claim: In type 2 diabetes insulin is usually high, not low; the problem is that cells resist it.
why: Type 1 destroys insulin-making cells, so insulin is missing. Type 2 starts with resistance: the pancreas over-produces insulin to force sugar into unresponsive cells.

claim: Prescribed insulin lowers blood sugar but reliably adds weight, which tends to deepen type 2 diabetes over time.
why: Insulin is the body's main storage signal. More of it pushes energy into fat, and extra weight raises resistance, so doses keep climbing.
do: If you take insulin, never adjust it yourself; fasting with your doctor can lower the dose you need.
counter: Weight gain from insulin is well documented. "Treating T2D with insulin is exactly wrong" is Fung's view; insulin is still needed in many cases.

claim: Constantly high insulin may itself drive insulin resistance, the way any constant drug exposure builds tolerance.
why: Cells exposed to persistently high insulin down-regulate their response. Lowering insulin through fasting periods gives them a chance to resensitize.
counter: Shown in clamp studies over days; it is one cause among several (fat in liver and muscle, genetics, inactivity).
note: VERIFIED citation (PubMed).

claim: Type 2 diabetes can often be put into remission through diet. It is not necessarily a lifelong, progressive disease.
why: When liver and pancreas fat fall with sustained weight loss, insulin secretion and sensitivity can recover, especially early in the disease.
do: Remission is achievable; track it with your doctor through HbA1c, not by stopping medication on your own.
counter: DiRECT used a low-calorie diet, not fasting. Fasting-specific evidence is case series (Furmli 2018 BMJ Case Rep). Remission is less likely after many years of disease.

claim: Fasting is the simplest way to lower insulin. It needs no special foods, recipes or shopping.
why: Every food raises insulin to some degree. Not eating is the one approach that drops it for everyone, whatever their diet.

claim: Diet sodas during a fast tend to make hunger and cravings worse, not better.
why: Intense sweetness without energy may keep appetite and food reward primed. Many fasters report stronger cravings with sweeteners.
do: Drink water, tea instead of sweetened drinks.
counter: Human trials on sweeteners and appetite are mixed. This is mainly clinical experience.
note: Superseded by CGF-09-006 (better evidence); keep as anecdotal support.

claim: Fatigue and light-headedness while fasting are often low salt, not low energy.
why: Falling insulin makes the kidneys excrete sodium and water ("natriuresis of fasting"). Low sodium causes fatigue, dizziness and headache.
do: Add a pinch of salt to a glass of water.
note: VERIFIED: natriuresis of fasting (Spark 1975 NEJM; Boulter 1974 JCEM PMID 4812620).

claim: Hunger after a long fast can trigger heavy overeating. The first meal deserves a plan.
why: Pent-up hunger plus a sudden large meal overloads a gut that has been resting, causing pain and undoing the calm the fast created.
do: Break a fast with a small meal, wait 30–60 minutes, then eat normally.
note: Superseded by CGF-15-004 (canonical break-fast card).

claim: Day 2 is commonly the hardest. Hunger often fades after it rather than building.
why: Ghrelin and hunger follow learned meal times and peak early. As ketones rise around days 2–3, appetite usually drops.
do: If day 2 is rough, expect it to ease. Don't judge the whole fast by its hardest day.
counter: Mostly self-reported. Ghrelin data are covered in ch9 cards.

claim: Already eating low-carb makes fasting markedly easier, because the body is used to running on fat.
why: Glycogen holds roughly 2,000 kcal; even lean bodies store tens of thousands of kcal as fat. Fat-adapted people switch fuels without a hunger spike.
do: Before trying longer fasts, a few weeks of lower-carb eating can soften the transition.
counter: Fung also uses fasting successfully in people who aren't keto-adapted. Adaptation helps, but isn't required.

claim: Ketogenic eating often blunts appetite so much that people skip meals without trying.
why: Ketones and steady blood sugar suppress hunger hormones; fewer insulin swings mean fewer rebound cravings.

claim: Stop the fast if you feel truly unwell: energy gone and not returning, faint, or ravenous beyond normal hunger.
why: Normal hunger comes in waves and passes. Persistent weakness or feeling "not yourself" means the fast isn't right for you today.
do: End it, eat something, and try again in a week. Stopping isn't failing.

claim: Long fasts often fail during travel, stress or celebrations. Plan them around those events.
why: Fasting is itself a stressor. On top of other stress it shifts from beneficial (hormetic) to draining, and hunger rises.
do: Don't start a multi-day fast just before travel, a wedding or a demanding week. Short fasts are fine.

claim: Most of the scale drop in a week-long fast is water and stored glycogen, not fat.
why: Each gram of glycogen is stored with about 3 g of water. Emptying glycogen sheds 1–2 kg quickly, and much of it returns on refeeding.
do: Judge long fasts by the weight still off a few weeks later, not by the last day's number.

claim: Body scans during a fast can show "muscle loss" that is really water and glycogen, which returns after eating.
why: DXA counts water and glycogen as lean mass. In Moore's 28-day fast, scanned lean loss had fully recovered after two weeks of eating.
counter: n=1. Fung attributed it to organ fat; water/glycogen is the more standard explanation. Some real protein loss does occur, mostly early in a fast.

claim: During long fasts blood sugar typically settles around 60–75 mg/dL without symptoms. Readings in the 50s with weakness mean break the fast.
why: The liver keeps glucose low but steady and the brain shifts to ketones. Symptomatic lows mean that balance is failing.
do: If you're shaky, sweaty, confused or can barely stand, eat now, and measure if you have a meter.

claim: Most doctors receive only a few hours of nutrition training across years of medical education.
why: Fung estimates about four hours in nine years. US surveys show most schools fall below the recommended 25 hours.
note: true but not user-actionable; keep as context only.

claim: Prolonged fasting can temporarily raise LDL cholesterol in lean people, even though it improves most metabolic markers.
why: Fat mobilized from stores circulates as lipoproteins. Lean fasters show the largest rise, which reverses after refeeding.
counter: Moore's n=1 showed a large LDL drop (he was overweight). Results depend on body fat and timing of the test.
note: VERIFIED title: fasting increases total cholesterol, LDL, apoB in healthy nonobese humans.

claim: Fasting is voluntary and can end any moment you choose; starvation is forced, with no control and no end in sight.
why: The physiology overlaps, but control changes everything: you start when ready, carry stored fuel, and stop at will.

claim: Everyone already fasts daily. "Breakfast" literally means the meal that breaks the overnight fast.
why: Any time you aren't eating, you're fasting; deliberate fasting just extends a normal daily state.

claim: Adults now eat about 5–6 times a day, up from about 3 in the late 1970s. The daily fasting window has nearly vanished.
why: With 3 meals, ~14 h of each day was fasted. Constant snacking keeps insulin up most waking hours, leaving little time to burn stores.
do: Cutting snacks is the first, easiest fast. Three meals with nothing between already restores a daily low-insulin window.
src: Popkin & Duffey 2010 Am J Clin Nutr
counter: Eating frequency rose alongside obesity; that it causes obesity is not proven.
note: Gill & Panda: more than half of adults spread eating over 15 h or more per day.

claim: Protein raises insulin too. Some proteins (whey, beef) raise it about as much as some starchy foods; fat raises it least.
why: Amino acids stimulate insulin release directly. Fat barely does, but fat is rarely eaten alone.
counter: Protein also raises glucagon, which offsets some effects; protein is highly satiating and needed for muscle.

claim: The body has two modes: fed (insulin high, storing energy) and fasted (insulin low, burning stores). Weight follows the balance of time between them.
why: Insulin is the switch. Long fed periods favor storage; regular fasted periods let stored glycogen and fat be spent.
do: Think in time, not just calories: aim for real stretches each day where insulin can fall.
counter: A useful model; energy balance still applies, and calories within the eating window still matter.

claim: Liver glycogen covers roughly a day of glucose needs. As it runs down, the liver makes new glucose and fat burning takes over.
why: The liver holds ~100 g glycogen. Gluconeogenesis rises within hours and supplies most glucose by ~22 h, fueled partly by glycerol from fat.
counter: Fung says glycogen lasts 24–36 h; Rothman shows gluconeogenesis already ~64% of output in the first 22 h. Timing varies with prior meals and activity.
note: STAGE AUDIT: app's 8–12 h "gluconeogenesis" and 12–18 h "fat burning" fit Rothman better than Fung's 24 h–2 d. Keep app timing; cite Rothman.

claim: After a few days of fasting, ketones supply a large share of the brain's energy, sparing glucose and therefore muscle protein.
why: Fat can't cross into the brain, but liver-made ketones can. Blood β-hydroxybutyrate can rise over 70-fold, cutting the brain's need for glucose.
counter: Fung says ~75% at 4 days. Owen measured ~60–70% after 5–6 weeks; at day 3–4 the share is lower, closer to a third or half.

claim: Protein breakdown is highest in the first days of fasting, then drops sharply as ketones take over. It falls; it never stops.
why: Early glucose comes partly from amino acids. As ketones rise, nitrogen loss falls to a fraction, sparing muscle.
counter: Fung says that from day 5 protein "is not being used for energy". It is used, at a low rate (about 20–30 g protein/day).

claim: Lowering insulin makes the kidneys shed salt and water. Early weight drop, less bloating and lower blood pressure are common.
why: Insulin signals the kidneys to retain sodium. When it falls, sodium and water leave, which also lowers blood pressure.
do: If you take blood-pressure pills or diuretics, ask your doctor first. Fasting can push pressure too low.

claim: Blood electrolytes usually stay in normal range even in very long supervised fasts; the body guards them tightly.
why: Bones hold 99% of calcium, magnesium and phosphorus, and the kidneys cut losses. Potassium may dip slightly but stays normal.
do: For fasts longer than a few days, a multivitamin and salt cover the gaps; supervised fasts check blood levels.
counter: Normal blood levels don't prove normal body stores. In the 382-day fast, potassium needed correcting early and plasma magnesium stayed low throughout (Stewart & Fleming 1973, PMID 4803438). The real danger comes at refeeding (ch14).
note: VERIFIED Stewart & Fleming abstract. Drenick 1964 complications still unchecked.

claim: Children, pregnant and breastfeeding women should not fast for health; their mineral and energy needs are ongoing.
why: Growth, pregnancy and milk production need a continuous supply of nutrients that body stores shouldn't be drawn down to cover.
do: If you're pregnant, breastfeeding or under 18, don't use extended fasting.

claim: Metabolism tends to rise slightly in short fasts. Resting energy use was up ~12% after four days without food.
why: Noradrenaline rises to release stored fuel and keep you alert, so you have the energy to find food rather than shutting down.
do: Expect alertness, not sluggishness, on days 2–4. Fatigue usually signals low salt, not a slowing metabolism.
counter: Small study (n=11) of lean adults. Much longer fasts do eventually reduce energy expenditure.

claim: Fasting is the strongest natural booster of growth hormone: about 5-fold over a 2-day fast.
why: Meals and high insulin suppress GH. Without food its pulses get bigger and more frequent, which helps release fat and limit muscle-protein breakdown.
counter: Fasting GH is a fuel-sparing signal, not an anti-aging or anabolic one. IGF-1 falls at the same time. Small studies in lean men.
note: STAGE AUDIT: app attributes "5-fold over ~2 days" to Ho 1988. Ho 1988 = 5-day fast (~2x+ integrated GH). The 2-day 5-fold figure is Hartman 1992. Fix the citation.

claim: A large meal can suppress growth hormone by as much as 80%.
why: Overeating raises insulin sharply, and high insulin is a strong brake on growth-hormone release.

claim: The body's hormones peak around 4 a.m., releasing sugar before you wake. Morning blood sugar can rise without food.
why: Growth hormone, cortisol and adrenaline counter insulin to prepare fuel for the day: the "dawn phenomenon".
do: A higher morning reading while fasting is normal and not a sign the fast is failing.

claim: Ultra-processed food makes people eat more. In a controlled trial, it added ~500 kcal/day compared with whole foods matched for nutrients.
why: Processing strips fiber and structure, speeds eating and absorption, and weakens fullness signals, so the same "macros" behave very differently.
do: Break fasts and fill eating windows with recognizable whole foods; avoid packaged products.

claim: Sugar and refined flour are the foods most worth cutting; they raise insulin most and fill you least.
why: Finely milled, fiber-stripped carbohydrates absorb fast, spike glucose and insulin, and leave hunger soon after.
counter: Low-carb and low-fat diets come out similar for weight in long RCTs (DIETFITS, Gardner 2018 JAMA). Food quality matters more than macro ratios, which is Fung's point too.

claim: Industrial trans fats harm the heart; natural fats in olive oil, nuts, avocado and fish are protective.
why: Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL. Mediterranean-style fats reduced cardiovascular events in a large RCT.

claim: Fung considers seed oils (corn, sunflower, canola) inflammatory because of their omega-6 content.
why: His view: modern diets carry far more omega-6 than omega-3, tipping the balance toward inflammation.
counter: Controlled trials find dietary linoleic acid does not raise inflammatory markers, and it's linked to lower heart risk. Contested; not for in-app claims.
note: Johnson & Fritsche 2012 J Acad Nutr Diet; Farvid 2014 Circulation. Keep for audit only.

claim: Dry fasting (no food and no water) is harder and riskier, and adds no health benefit over a water fast.
why: Dehydration adds strain on kidneys and blood pressure, limits safe duration, and raises complication risk without improving the metabolic effects.
do: On religious dry-fast days keep them short; health fasts should always include water.
note: Links to the lunar/Ekadashi feature (nirjala fasts are dry).

claim: While fasting, water and plain or herbal tea are all fine.
why: They carry little or no energy, so insulin stays low, while easing hunger and supplying fluid and salt.

claim: PCOS is closely tied to insulin resistance, and lowering insulin can restore cycles and reduce symptoms.
why: High insulin drives the ovaries to overproduce androgens. Reducing it is a first-line approach, and weight loss often restores ovulation.
counter: Fasting-specific PCOS trials are small; the link to insulin resistance is well established.

claim: Nearly every religious tradition sets regular fast days. Weekly, lunar and seasonal fasts form a built-in intermittent-fasting calendar.
why: Hindu lunar and weekday fasts, Orthodox Christian fasts on up to 180–200 days a year, Buddhist monks eating nothing after noon, Ramadan, and Monday/Thursday fasts in Islam.
note: Anchors the app's lunar/Ekadashi feature in the wider tradition.

claim: Crete, the original model for the "Mediterranean diet", was also a population that fasted on many days of the year under Orthodox tradition.
why: Ancel Keys's studies of Crete focused on food choices; the frequent fasting practised there was largely left out of the story.
counter: Whether fasting contributed to Cretan longevity is speculation.

claim: Ramadan is the most studied religious fast, but unlike health fasts it forbids fluids, causing daily mild dehydration.
why: Sunrise-to-sunset dry fasting combines food restriction with fluid restriction, so its research results don't map directly onto water fasts.

claim: Hippocrates advised people with obesity to eat only once a day. Plutarch, Paracelsus and Franklin all praised fasting as medicine.
why: Ancient physicians saw fasting as the body's own remedy; Paracelsus called it "the physician within".

claim: Losing appetite when ill is a shared instinct across mammals; the body deliberately turns hunger down during infection.
why: Sickness-induced anorexia frees energy and shifts metabolism toward defense. Fasting is one of the body's own responses, not an artificial imposition.
counter: In mice, fasting helped survival in bacterial infection but harmed it in viral infection. Don't force fasting during illness.

claim: Medicine used supervised fasting for obesity in the 1950s–60s, including absolute fasts of 14 days or more.
why: Bloom (1959), Gilliland (1968) and Drenick (1964) reported steady weight loss in hospital. Interest faded with the turn toward dietary-fat research.
counter: Fung leaves out that some prolonged therapeutic fasts ended in serious complications and a few deaths (see SCI-02-001).

claim: Very long water-only fasts carried real risks in the 1960s hospital programs: rare cardiac deaths and serious complications.
why: Reports included heart-muscle damage, dangerous arrhythmias, lactic acidosis and severe refeeding problems, mostly in fasts of many weeks without monitoring.
do: Never fast beyond about 3 days alone. Longer fasts need medical supervision and blood tests.
note: VERIFIED all three exist (titles: cardiac myofibril fragmentation; death during therapeutic starvation; 'a dangerous procedure?').

claim: Months of daily calorie cutting lower your metabolism substantially: the "starvation mode" people fear from fasting.
why: In long calorie-restricted studies metabolic rate fell 25–40%, partly from lost mass and partly from adaptation. Cold, fatigue and hunger follow, so weight returns easily.
counter: Some of the drop simply reflects a smaller body. The adaptive part beyond that is real but smaller, around 5–15%.

claim: Three weeks of alternate-day fasting did not lower resting metabolism. Fat burning rose ~58% while sugar burning fell ~53%.
why: The body switched fuel, not throttle: stored fat replaced dietary carbohydrate, and total energy use held steady.
counter: 22 days, 16 non-obese adults. Longer RCTs find alternate-day fasting about equal to daily calorie restriction for weight (Trepanowski 2017 JAMA Intern Med).

claim: In a 10-week alternate-day fasting study, about 6% weight loss came almost entirely from fat; lean mass didn't change.
why: Fat mass fell ~11% while fat-free mass held. Intermittent fasting appeared to spare lean tissue in this trial.
counter: Small trial. Other studies find lean loss similar to calorie restriction (~25% of weight lost), and higher in some time-restricted eating trials (Lowe 2020 JAMA Intern Med).

claim: Fung says the body only turns to muscle when body fat is nearly gone (under ~4%).
why: His reasoning: fat is the energy store and muscle is functional tissue, so evolution should protect muscle until fat runs out.
counter: Not supported as stated. Protein is broken down from the first day at a falling rate; it is spared, not untouched (see CGF-01-008).
note: Do not ship. Kept so the claim's correction is on record.

claim: Resistance exercise and enough protein while eating are what protect muscle; fasting doesn't replace either.
why: Muscle responds to load. Combining fasting or time-restricted eating with strength training preserves lean mass far better than fasting alone.
do: Lift or do bodyweight training 2–3×/week, and eat ample protein (~1.2–1.6 g/kg) within your eating window.
counter: Fung says supplements like whey and creatine don't build muscle; meta-analyses show modest added gains when combined with training.

claim: Blocking growth hormone during a fast raises protein breakdown by about 50%. GH is one reason muscle is spared.
why: The fasting surge in growth hormone shifts fuel use toward fat and restrains muscle-protein breakdown.

claim: In healthy people fasting doesn't cause dangerous low blood sugar; the liver keeps glucose in range, overnight and for days.
why: Glycogen covers the first day; then the liver makes new glucose from glycerol and amino acids while ketones feed the brain.
do: If you take insulin, sulfonylureas or other glucose-lowering drugs, fasting can cause severe lows: get a medication plan from your doctor first.

claim: The brain is not glucose-only. Once fat-burning is under way it runs largely on ketones, so long fasts don't starve your thinking.
why: Ketones cross into the brain and replace much of its glucose need, the human brain's backup fuel for food scarcity.

claim: Many fasters report clear-headedness and calm in fasts. Ketones and a steadier fuel supply are the likely reason.
why: Ketone metabolism and the absence of blood-sugar swings may stabilize energy and mood; noradrenaline adds alertness.
counter: Mostly self-report. Small studies note mood improvement in fasting (Fond 2013 Psychiatry Res), but placebo and expectation effects are large.

claim: After a 36-hour fast, people eat only ~20% more the next day, leaving a net deficit of ~2,000 kcal over the two days.
why: Compensation is partial. Hunger after a fast doesn't come close to replacing the skipped meals.
do: Don't fear a rebound: eat normally after a fast, without "making up" for it.

claim: With regular fasting, appetite tends to fall over time rather than rise.
why: Clinical experience across hundreds of patients: hunger habituates as fasting becomes routine and insulin levels drop.

claim: There is no essential dietary carbohydrate. The body can make all the glucose it needs; essential amino acids and fats must come from food.
why: The liver synthesizes glucose; it can't make essential amino acids or omega-3/6 fats, so those need to be eaten between fasts.
do: Make your eating windows protein- and nutrient-rich; for fasts beyond a few days, take a multivitamin.

claim: Even a lean adult carries enough body fat to cover over a month of energy needs.
why: A 70 kg person at 15% body fat stores about 10 kg of fat, ~80,000 kcal, versus ~2,000 kcal of glycogen.
note: Fung/Abel James: "enough to walk from New York to Florida". Same idea, verifiable numbers.

claim: Skipping one day of meals means missing 3 of about 1,000 meals a year, too few to harm a healthy body.
why: The perspective counters the idea that a single missed meal is dangerous; metabolism doesn't shut down after one day.

claim: The whole method fits in one sentence: eat nothing; drink water or tea.
why: Diets often fail because they're confusing to follow. A rule this simple is hard to get wrong, and adherence is what produces results.

claim: Fasting costs nothing and saves time: no shopping, cooking or cleanup.
why: Healthy food can be expensive and time-consuming. Fasting removes both barriers and works for people on any budget.

claim: Feasts and fasts are meant to alternate. A planned fast after a celebration lets you enjoy it without guilt.
why: Humans have always paired feast days with fasting. Balance over the week matters more than any single meal.
do: Enjoy the wedding or holiday meal, then schedule a fast in the days after. Don't let a feast end your routine.

claim: Fasting is fully flexible: move a fast day, shorten it, or stop within minutes if you feel unwell.
why: Unlike surgery or fixed meal plans, nothing is locked in. Rescheduling around important days keeps fasting sustainable.
do: If a fast clashes with an important meeting or event, move it; consistency over weeks beats rigid days.

claim: Fasting works alongside any diet: vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, allergies, travel, old age, trouble chewing.
why: It takes away rather than adds, so no food rule clashes with it.

claim: When weight stalls, Fung's lever is fasting "dose": longer or more frequent fasts, rather than switching diets.
why: Low-carb or low-fat diets bottom out at zero carbs or fat; fasting time can be extended until the effect appears.
do: Plateaued? Add one longer fast a week or another fasting day before changing your whole approach.
counter: Risk rises with duration. Beyond about 3 days, medical supervision applies (see SCI-02-001). Fung's "no upper limit" is a therapeutic framing, not a safety claim.

claim: Fung lists fasting as preventing Alzheimer's, extending life and reversing aging.
why: These rest on animal studies and mechanisms (autophagy, insulin, inflammation) rather than human outcome trials.
counter: No human trial shows fasting prevents dementia or extends lifespan. Don't present these as established benefits.
note: Keep for audit. Any in-app longevity copy must be framed as "studied in animals".

claim: Sustained intermittent fasting typically lowers inflammation (CRP), blood sugar, HbA1c and blood pressure.
why: Fat loss plus long low-insulin periods improve the main markers of metabolic health.
src: de Cabo & Mattson 2019 N Engl J Med
counter: Effects are largely explained by weight loss; versus equal-calorie daily restriction, results are similar.

claim: Weight regain after dieting is biology, not weak willpower. Nearly every calorie-cutting diet plateaus and rebounds.
why: In a UK cohort of ~175,000 obese adults, under 1% reached normal weight per year. In a huge 7-year trial, women cutting ~360 kcal/day ended up less than 1 kg lighter.
do: If past diets failed, it wasn't a character flaw. Change the strategy, not your self-judgment.

claim: Six years after The Biggest Loser, most contestants had regained the weight, and they still burned ~700 kcal/day less than expected.
why: Large, sustained calorie deficits provoke lasting metabolic adaptation: the body defends its former weight by spending less energy.
counter: n=14. Adaptation tracked the degree of energy deficit and leptin rather than insulin (Knuth 2014 Obesity).

claim: Glycogen is a fridge; body fat is a basement freezer. You mostly use the fridge first, and insulin decides whether the freezer door is open.
why: Glycogen is small and quick to access; fat is vast and slower. High insulin blocks fat release; low insulin unlocks it, even before glycogen is fully empty.
do: Every hour after insulin falls and the "fridge" empties is an hour you're drawing on the freezer. That's what fasting buys.
counter: Insulin's block on fat release is textbook (A). Fung's broader claim that insulin, not energy balance, is the root cause of obesity is contested (Hall 2015 Cell Metab).

claim: Insulin is the brake on fat burning. Even modest insulin levels sharply suppress the release of fat from fat cells.
why: Insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase. Fat cells release fatty acids freely only when insulin is low.

claim: Before insulin was discovered, children with type 1 diabetes wasted away however much they ate. It shows insulin's power over fat storage.
why: With no insulin, fat is released constantly and can't be stored. Insulin injections restored normal weight within weeks (1922).

claim: After weight loss, appetite rises by roughly 100 kcal/day for every kilogram lost: about three times more than metabolism slows.
why: The body defends its prior weight mostly through hunger. That's why maintenance feels harder than the loss itself.
do: Expect stronger hunger after losing weight. Regular fasting and protein-rich, unprocessed meals help hold the line.
note: VERIFIED citation; derived from SGLT2-inhibitor trial data modelling energy intake.

claim: In type 2 diabetes, a carb-free diet delivered about 71% of the glucose-lowering benefit of a fast, at equal calories.
why: Removing carbohydrate removes most of the insulin stimulus. Fasting also removes protein's insulin effect, cutting insulin further.
do: If low-carb alone has stalled your blood sugar, intermittent fasting is the next lever (with your doctor if on medication).
counter: Short study, small n. Shows glucose effects, not long-term outcomes.

claim: Two low-calorie days a week (5:2) gave the same weight loss as daily calorie cutting but a larger improvement in insulin sensitivity.
why: Total weekly calories were nearly equal; the intermittent pattern produced deeper, repeated low-insulin periods.
counter: n=107 women, 6 months. Later trials show mostly similar metabolic effects at equal weight loss. The insulin advantage is modest and not always replicated.

claim: Restricting some foods all of the time is a different strategy from restricting all foods some of the time.
why: Constant restriction invites constant adaptation. Intermittent restriction alternates states, which may resist the body's adjustment.
counter: A useful framing; head-to-head trials show similar weight loss. The edge is in adherence and insulin, not magic.

claim: Surgically removing 10 kg of fat by liposuction gave no improvement in blood sugar, insulin action or heart-risk markers.
why: Metabolic harm comes from fat in the liver, muscle and around organs, and from high insulin, not from the amount of fat under the skin.

claim: Diabetes often improves within days after bariatric surgery, and an equally restrictive diet without surgery does as well or better.
why: The early benefit comes largely from the sudden, severe drop in food intake: in effect, enforced fasting.
counter: Long-term weight outcomes still favor surgery for severe obesity. Fasting isn't proven equivalent over years.

claim: Ketosis from fasting is normal and safe; diabetic ketoacidosis is a different, dangerous state that needs a severe lack of insulin.
why: In ketosis, insulin is low but present and ketones are burned as fuel. In ketoacidosis, almost no insulin lets ketones and glucose pile up to toxic levels.
do: Type 1 diabetes, or SGLT2-inhibitor drugs (names ending in "-gliflozin"): don't fast without your doctor, since ketoacidosis can occur even with normal sugar.
counter: Fung says non-diabetics can't develop ketoacidosis. Rare exceptions exist, e.g. lactation ketoacidosis in breastfeeding women.

claim: Short and intermittent fasts generally don't raise cortisol, the stress hormone. Most people feel no stress-hormone effect.
why: Two weeks of intermittent fasting left cortisol unchanged, and 72-hour fasts show little change.
do: If fasting leaves you wired, anxious or sleepless, shorten fasts or change approach.
counter: Five-day fasts can amplify cortisol release (Bergendahl 1996 J Clin Endocrinol Metab). Individual responses vary; Fung notes some patients.

claim: Real fat loss while fasting is about 0.25 kg (½ lb) per day. Anything faster is water, which returns when you eat.
why: A full day's energy need (~2,000 kcal) divided by ~7,700 kcal per kg of fat comes to about a quarter-kilo. The rest of a 1 kg drop is glycogen and its water.
do: Read the scale through this lens: water returns on eating, but the quarter-kilo of fat per fasted day is real progress.

claim: Plateaus are expected: weight lost on fasting days eventually balances weight regained on eating days.
why: Any steady routine reaches equilibrium. Changing the stimulus restarts progress.
do: Change the pattern: 24 h → 36 h → 48 h, one meal a day, or an occasional longer fast. Also check snacking and food quality.

claim: The longer you've been overweight, and if you take insulin, the slower fasting results tend to come. Persistence matters more than speed.
why: Long-standing insulin resistance and injected insulin keep fat stores harder to access, so early progress can be slow.

claim: More than half of US adults have diabetes or prediabetes, and most people with prediabetes don't know it.
why: In 2012, 14% had diabetes and 38% prediabetes. Prediabetes rarely causes symptoms, so it goes unnoticed for years.
do: Ask for an HbA1c or fasting glucose test at your next check-up, especially if you carry weight around the waist.

claim: Before insulin existed, the best diabetes treatment was supervised fasting followed by a very low-carb diet.
why: Allen and Joslin (1915–1921) found that fasting cleared sugar from the urine of many patients, likely those with type 2.
counter: Children with type 1 diabetes often died of starvation on it, which is why fasting is unsafe for type 1 and underweight people.

claim: Diabetes deaths fell sharply during wartime food rationing in both world wars, and rose again once rationing ended.
why: Sustained, population-wide calorie restriction lowered blood sugar and weight; the rebound followed normal eating, even after insulin arrived.
counter: Ecological data, confounded by wartime changes in activity, survival and record-keeping.

claim: Fat in the liver, pancreas and around organs drives type 2 diabetes far more than fat under the skin. Fasting tends to clear it first.
why: Fat in the liver causes insulin resistance there; fat in the pancreas impairs insulin release. Losing it can restore normal glucose control.
note: Taylor's "twin cycle" (liver + pancreas fat) is the best-supported mechanism behind remission.

claim: Fung pictures insulin resistance as an overfull subway train: the cell is already stuffed with fuel, so insulin can't push more sugar in.
why: In his model, excess stored energy overflows into the blood. The cure is to empty the cell (eat less, burn more), not to push harder with more insulin.
counter: The analogy matches the lipid-overload model (fat in liver and muscle blocks insulin signaling) rather than glucose literally overfilling cells.

claim: Fasting while on diabetes medication without a plan can cause dangerous low blood sugar: shaking, sweating, confusion, even loss of consciousness.
why: Most diabetes drugs lower sugar on the assumption that you'll eat. Remove the food and the same dose overshoots.
do: See your doctor before fasting on insulin or diabetes pills. Expect your doses to change on fasting days.

claim: If you fast while on glucose-lowering drugs, check your blood sugar 2–4 times a day, on fasting and eating days.
why: Changes come fast and vary by drug; frequent checks let you and your doctor catch lows early and adjust doses.
do: Treat a low (under ~4 mmol/L, 70 mg/dL) with sugar right away, even if it ends the fast, and tell your doctor.

claim: Fung's clinic prefers slightly high sugar on fasting days to any risk of a low: about 8–10 mmol/L (145–180 mg/dL) while on medication.
why: Short-term mild highs are harmless while fasting brings sugar down; a low is acutely dangerous and breaks the fast.
do: Agree target ranges and a "less medication on fast days" plan with your own doctor. Don't adopt these numbers alone.

claim: If you aren't on glucose-lowering medication, there's no need to monitor blood sugar during fasting; it stays in the normal range.
why: Without drugs pushing sugar down, the liver keeps glucose steady through glycogen and gluconeogenesis.

claim: A fast that ends early still counts. Stopping at 22 of 24 planned hours is 22 hours of benefit, not a failure.
why: Benefits accumulate hour by hour. Treating short attempts as wins builds the confidence that makes longer fasts possible.
do: End when you need to, log what you did, and try again; each attempt gets easier.
note: Supports the app's non-punitive tone (red countdowns already removed).

claim: Staying busy is one of the most effective ways to get through early fasts.
why: Hunger is largely triggered by cues and boredom. Engaged attention leaves less room for food thoughts.
do: Schedule fasts on work days rather than idle days; plan an activity for the usual mealtime.

claim: Short fasts don't dull your mind. Controlled studies found no loss of attention, reaction time, memory or mood over up to two days.
why: The brain is protected first during food scarcity; ketones and noradrenaline keep it fueled and alert.
do: You can work, study and drive normally on fasting days. If you feel foggy, check salt and fluids first.
counter: Some studies find mild irritability or slower performance on specific tasks early in fasting, especially in first-time fasters.

claim: In famine, mammals shrink most organs but protect the brain. Mental sharpness is defended because it's needed to find food.
why: Evolution favored animals that stayed alert when hungry; losing focus during scarcity would compound the danger.

claim: Post-feast sleepiness comes from the sheer size of the meal, not from tryptophan in the turkey.
why: Turkey has no more tryptophan than other poultry. Large meals trigger hormonal and nervous-system shifts that favor rest and digestion.
counter: Fung blames blood being diverted from the brain; brain blood flow is tightly regulated, so hormonal and vagal effects are the better explanation.

claim: In animals, intermittent fasting improves learning and memory and slows brain aging, partly by raising BDNF, a nerve-growth factor.
why: Both fasting and exercise raise BDNF in rodent brains. Fasted mice show fewer signs of Alzheimer's-, Parkinson's- and Huntington's-like disease.
counter: Animal data. Human trials on fasting and long-term cognition are small and inconclusive.

claim: Older adults who cut calories by 30% for three months improved their memory scores in a controlled study.
why: Memory gains tracked falling insulin and inflammation, suggesting metabolic health supports brain function.
src: Witte 2009 Proc Natl Acad Sci USA
counter: n=50, 3 months, calorie restriction rather than fasting; not replicated at scale.

claim: Autophagy is the cell's recycling system: it breaks down worn-out proteins and parts and reuses the material.
why: When nutrients are scarce, cells dismantle their oldest components for fuel and building blocks, clearing damage that otherwise builds up with age.

claim: Eating, especially protein and carbohydrate, switches autophagy off through the mTOR nutrient sensor; constant snacking keeps it suppressed.
why: Insulin and amino acids activate mTOR, which tells cells food is plentiful and blocks recycling. Fat stores don't count; only incoming nutrients do.
do: Long gaps between meals, with no snacking, give cells time with mTOR switched off.
counter: Fung's "3 g of leucine stops autophagy" cites a muscle-growth study (Glynn 2010), not one measuring autophagy. The direction is right; the threshold is unproven.

claim: Fasting increases autophagy in humans, but nobody knows when it starts or peaks. Popular "16 h" or "24 h" thresholds come from animal studies.
why: Human autophagy can't yet be measured directly in living tissue. Markers rise in muscle and blood after 24–36 h fasts and with time-restricted eating.
counter: Fung presents fasting as the strongest autophagy trigger. Plausible, but human evidence is indirect, and calorie restriction also induces autophagy in animals.
note: STAGE AUDIT: app's 24–48 h autophagy copy already hedges ("human timing still mapped"). The "Optimal autophagy" notification and the "Autophagy: N hours" log totals imply measured precision; flag for review.

claim: In Alzheimer's, the brain's autophagy system fails to clear amyloid protein clumps; boosting autophagy is a research target.
why: Brain cells normally package amyloid-beta for disposal through autophagy. When the pathway stalls, amyloid accumulates inside neurons.
counter: That fasting prevents Alzheimer's in people is unproven.

claim: Fasting is not a cancer treatment. With cancer, fast only under your oncologist; the relationship between autophagy and cancer cuts both ways.
why: Autophagy can prevent cancer from starting but can also help established tumors survive stress. Weight loss can be dangerous during cancer therapy.
do: If you have cancer or are in treatment, don't fast without your oncology team. Some trials study fasting-mimicking diets alongside chemo.
counter: Fung cites Seyfried's annual 7-day fast for cancer prevention; that is a hypothesis without human outcome data.

claim: Multi-day fasts in mice clear old immune cells and trigger regeneration from stem cells when refeeding begins.
why: Prolonged fasting lowers IGF-1 and PKA signaling, pushing blood stem cells to self-renew. Refeeding rebuilds a younger immune population.
counter: Mostly mouse data; human evidence is a small pilot in chemotherapy patients. "Immune reset" in healthy people is unproven.
note: STAGE AUDIT: app's 72 h+ stage presents this as human fact; reword to "in animal studies" and keep the Cheng citation.

claim: Triglycerides, a blood fat made by the liver from excess carbohydrate, predict heart risk almost as strongly as LDL.
why: When glycogen is full, the liver turns surplus sugar into triglycerides, exported as VLDL, the precursor of LDL. Cutting refined carbs and fasting lower them quickly.

claim: For most people, cholesterol in food (eggs, shellfish) has only a small effect on blood cholesterol; the liver makes most of it.
why: The liver produces roughly 80% of blood cholesterol and makes less when more is eaten.
counter: About a quarter of people are "hyper-responders". Saturated fat (not dietary cholesterol) does raise LDL in controlled feeding trials (Mensink 2016 WHO).

claim: Fung argues dietary fat doesn't raise blood cholesterol and that low-fat guidelines were never supported by trials.
why: He cites Framingham's unpublished diet data, Tecumseh and Harcombe's 2015 meta-analysis of the trials available in 1977–83.
counter: Saturated fat raises LDL in controlled feeding studies, and replacing it with unsaturated fat lowers heart events. Contested; not for in-app claims.
note: Keep for audit only.

claim: In a 10-week alternate-day fasting trial, LDL fell ~25% and triglycerides ~30%, while protective HDL held steady.
why: Less incoming carbohydrate means the liver makes fewer triglycerides and less VLDL, the source of LDL. Fat loss improves the whole lipid profile.
counter: Small trial in obese adults, largely mediated by weight loss. Lean people can see LDL rise during prolonged fasts (CGF-00-019).

claim: Fasting can improve blood pressure, sugar and lipids, but it's not a reason to stop prescribed heart or cholesterol medication on your own.
why: Medications protect against events that fasting's improvements may not fully cover yet. Doses should be reduced deliberately, with monitoring.
do: Share your fasting plan with your doctor and let them taper statins or blood-pressure drugs if your numbers improve.
counter: Fung highlights statin side effects (diabetes risk is real but small; the Alzheimer's link isn't supported).

claim: Hunger comes in waves, not a steady climb. A wave builds, peaks and fades, often within an hour, even if you eat nothing.
why: Ghrelin, the hunger hormone, spikes around your usual mealtimes and then drops again on its own, whether or not food arrives.
do: When a wave hits, drink something warm (tea or hot water), wait 20–30 minutes, and move on to a task. It passes.

claim: Morning is usually the least hungry time of day, even after 12–14 hours without food. Evening is the hungriest.
why: Appetite follows the body clock: the circadian drive for hunger is lowest around 8 a.m. and highest around 8 p.m., regardless of when you last ate.
do: Extending the overnight fast by skipping breakfast is often the easiest first step.

claim: Much of what we call hunger is learned. Clocks, places, screens and smells can trigger it like Pavlov's bell.
why: Repeated pairing of food with times and situations conditions the brain to release saliva, insulin and hunger signals on cue: the cephalic phase response.
do: Notice the trigger ("it's noon", "I'm on the couch") and label it: cue, not need.

claim: Eating only at a table, never at the desk, in the car, in bed or in front of a screen, unwires many hunger cues.
why: When food is tied to one place, other places stop triggering it. This was ordinary habit for earlier generations.

claim: Swap a habit rather than just dropping it. Replace the evening snack with a cup of herbal or green tea.
why: Stopping a routine leaves a gap that pulls you back; substituting a harmless ritual keeps the cue but changes the response, as gum does for ex-smokers.
do: Pick one replacement ritual for your usual snack time and keep it for two weeks.

claim: Diet drinks and sweeteners can make fasting harder; replacing diet drinks with water led to more weight loss in a 24-week trial.
why: Sweet taste may trigger the cephalic hunger and insulin response without supplying energy, leaving appetite primed but unsatisfied.
do: Fast without sweeteners if you can. If you need some, use a little, and drop it if hunger worsens or progress stalls.
counter: Whether sweeteners themselves trigger insulin in humans is inconsistent across studies; effects vary by person and sweetener.

claim: Smelling, seeing or cooking food while fasting is the hardest test there is. Avoid it rather than resist it.
why: Food cues fully trigger the cephalic hunger response. Failing to resist it is physiology, not weak willpower.
do: Don't cook, browse food or shop on fasting days; leave the kitchen during family meals if you need to.

claim: Keep your rituals on fasting days: a cup of tea at your usual breakfast and dinner times.
why: The habit of consuming something at those times is kept, so the cue is met even though the meal is skipped.

claim: Write an if-then list for hunger moments, e.g. "If I open the fridge, I walk for ten minutes instead."
why: Pre-planned responses to a specific cue ("implementation intentions") reliably beat willpower in behavior research.
do: Keep 3–5 quick actions ready: water, a walk, a call, a small chore, stepping outside.
note: Strong phase-2 candidate: a user-editable "when hunger hits" list surfaced from the hunger trigger.

claim: In longer fasts hunger typically peaks around day 2 and then fades. Many people feel unusually well afterward.
why: Hunger is hormonal, not a gauge of an empty stomach. As ketones rise, appetite signals quiet down; hospital fasting reports note little hunger after the first days.

claim: Fung sometimes advises people stuck at 24 hours to try a 3–7 day fast: once day 2 passes, they learn first-hand that hunger fades.
why: A longer fast lets the body fully switch to fat and ketones, which resets expectations about hunger faster than repeated short attempts.
counter: Done under his clinic's supervision. Not for anyone on glucose-lowering drugs or doing it unsupervised for the first time (see SCI-02-001).

claim: Don't fast if you're underweight or malnourished. Fung advises against any fasting below a BMI of about 20.
why: Without enough fat to draw on, the body breaks down functional tissue; complication risk climbs steeply at low body weight.
do: Check your BMI (weight in kg ÷ height in m²). Under 20, don't use fasting for health.

claim: If you have or have had an eating disorder, don't fast. It can feed restriction or binge cycles.
why: Deliberate restriction overlaps with the core behaviors of anorexia and bulimia, and can trigger relapse in people with that history.
do: If food or weight feels out of control, talk to a professional before any fasting.
counter: Fung argues fasting doesn't cause anorexia, and in obese adults alternate-day fasting didn't raise disordered-eating scores. Risk is in those already vulnerable.

claim: Fasting shouldn't be punishment for overeating. Use it as a planned rhythm, not penance for "cheating".
why: Compensatory restriction after eating is a recognized risk pattern for disordered eating and erodes your relationship with food.
note: Tempers CGF-04-003 (feast then fast): frame as balance, never as atonement. Phase-2 copy must avoid "make up for" language.

claim: Uric acid rises during fasting, which can trigger gout in susceptible people. Talk to your doctor first if you've had gout.
why: Ketones compete with uric acid for excretion by the kidneys, so blood levels climb. In one study of 42 fasters, all rose but none developed gout.
do: With a gout history, stay well hydrated and ask whether to keep your uric-acid medication during fasts.

claim: Some medicines are harsh on an empty stomach: aspirin, metformin, iron and magnesium supplements are the usual culprits.
why: Aspirin irritates the stomach lining, metformin causes nausea or diarrhea, iron causes pain and constipation, magnesium causes diarrhea; food buffers all of them.
do: Ask your doctor or pharmacist whether to take these in your eating window. Never just skip prescribed medication.

claim: Know the signs of low blood sugar: shaking, sweating, nervousness, faintness, sudden hunger, nausea, then confusion or seizures.
why: On diabetes drugs, sugar can fall fast once food is removed. Untreated lows can be fatal.
do: If these appear, take sugar immediately (juice, glucose tablets), even if it ends the fast, then call your doctor.

claim: Heartburn can get worse while fasting because there's no food to absorb stomach acid, though for some people it improves.
why: Abdominal fat presses on the stomach; an empty stomach still secretes acid. Weight loss over time usually relieves reflux.
do: Stop eating 3 h before bed, walk after dinner, raise the head of the bed. Ask about antacids if needed.

claim: Women benefit from fasting as much as men; a 3-day fast left reproductive hormones and the menstrual cycle unchanged in normal-weight women.
why: Hormone disruption and lost periods come from low body fat and energy deficiency, not fasting in itself in women with adequate reserves.
counter: Small studies. Lean, very active women are at higher risk of energy deficiency (RED-S); women-specific long-term data are limited.

claim: If your period stops or becomes irregular while fasting, stop fasting and see your doctor.
why: Amenorrhea signals that energy availability has dropped too low for reproductive function: a clear sign the current approach is too much.

claim: Couples who fast together succeed most often, in Fung's clinic experience.
why: Shared schedules remove food cues at home, and mutual support helps through hard moments.
do: Invite a partner or friend to fast with you, or at least tell someone close what you're doing.

claim: Track the symptoms that matter to you. If they're trending better, continue; if worse over days, change the approach.
why: Responses to fasting vary; the global trend is more informative than any single good or bad day.
note: Phase-2 idea: optional per-fast note or mood/energy tag in the log.

claim: Epsom salt baths are a traditional way to get magnesium without stomach upset, though skin absorption is unproven.
why: Oral magnesium often causes diarrhea, especially on an empty stomach; Fung suggests soaking in Epsom salts as an alternative.
counter: Controlled evidence that magnesium is meaningfully absorbed through the skin is lacking (Gröber 2017 Nutrients).

claim: Allowed while fasting: still or sparkling water, any tea including herbal, and natural flavors like lemon, mint or cinnamon.
why: These carry almost no energy, so insulin stays low, while they ease hunger, keep you hydrated and preserve daily rituals.
note: Phase-2 candidate: a quick "Can I have…?" lookup from the fasting screen.

claim: Not allowed: sugar, honey, agave, juice, artificial sweeteners and flavors (diet drinks, flavored water mixes).
why: Sugars break the fast outright. Fung excludes sweeteners and artificial flavors because they can stoke hunger and run against the purpose of the fast.

claim: Aim for about 2 liters of fluid a day while fasting, and start each morning with a glass of water.
why: Part of normal fluid intake comes from food, so fasting removes it; losing salt and water when insulin falls adds to dehydration risk.

claim: Green tea may help suppress appetite during a fast; cinnamon and ginger teas are traditional hunger-quieters, and mint or chamomile calm.
why: Green-tea catechins are thought to influence appetite and fat metabolism; warm drinks also fill the stomach and satisfy the ritual.
counter: Human appetite data for catechins are weak and inconsistent; the calming, ritual effect is the reliable part.

claim: A little apple-cider vinegar in water may blunt the blood-sugar rise from the next meal.
why: Acetic acid appears to slow stomach emptying and improve muscle glucose uptake; small trials show lower post-meal glucose.
do: Always dilute it (1–2 tablespoons in a large glass) to protect teeth and throat.
counter: Small, short trials; the effect is modest.

claim: A strict water-only fast includes no salt, so it carries more risk of dehydration, especially beyond a couple of days.
why: Without salt the body holds less water; kidneys conserve sodium well, but long water-only fasts still risk dizziness and low blood pressure.
do: For fasts longer than ~2 days, add salt to your water unless your doctor has told you to restrict it.

claim: Fruit-juice "fasts" aren't fasts: the sugar keeps insulin up. Green vegetable juices carry far less sugar.
why: Fruit juices concentrate fructose and glucose without fiber, so they behave like sugary drinks.

claim: A "fat fast" (only cream, butter, coconut oil or a few nuts during the fast) is a soft option some people use to get through.
why: Pure fat barely raises insulin, and a small bite can rescue a fast that would otherwise be abandoned.
counter: Scientific evidence is scarce. It adds calories that delay drawing on body fat.

claim: The fasting-mimicking diet (5 days of ~700–1,100 kcal a month) aims to recreate fasting's effects while still eating.
why: Low protein and calorie intake lower IGF-1 and glucose much as fasting does, but with food provided.
counter: Fung considers it needlessly complex. It does have RCT data (3 monthly cycles improved weight and risk markers).

claim: There's no single best fasting schedule. The right one is the one you can repeat, and you can switch anytime.
why: Shorter daily fasts suit weight control and busy lives; longer, less frequent fasts act faster on blood sugar and fatty liver.

claim: The first few fasts are always the hardest. Fasting gets measurably easier with repetition.
why: Hunger habits, cephalic responses and fuel switching all adapt; your body learns to move into fat-burning faster.
do: Give it a month. Judge fasting by your fifth attempt, not your first.

claim: A 12-hour overnight fast (e.g. 7 p.m. to 7 a.m.) was normal until the 1970s. It's a good baseline for prevention.
why: It gives one daily low-insulin window. Fung considers it protective but usually not enough on its own to reverse weight gain.

claim: 16:8 (an 8-hour eating window, usually skipping breakfast) is the easiest daily fast to sustain, since sleep covers half of it.
why: Most people aren't hungry in the morning, so moving the first meal to midday creates a 16-hour fast with little effort.
do: Pair it with less sugar and refined carbs; Fung says the window alone works slowly.
counter: In RCTs, an 8-hour window alone gave little weight loss beyond normal eating (Lowe 2020). With equal calories it matched daily calorie restriction (Liu 2022 N Engl J Med).

claim: Time-restricted eating alone usually gives modest weight loss; benefits come mostly from eating less and better within the window.
why: Large RCTs (TREAT 2020, Liu 2022) found 16:8 or similar no better than equal-calorie eating without a window for weight.
do: Use the window as a structure, then fill it with whole, protein-rich food and no grazing.
counter: Earlier eating windows (early TRE) improved insulin sensitivity and blood pressure even without weight loss (Sutton 2018 Cell Metab).
note: Counterweight to Fung's TRE optimism; keeps in-app claims honest.

claim: An appetite reset from fasting only lasts while the schedule is kept, but a day or two off doesn't erase it.
why: Hunger patterns adapt to routine over weeks; brief breaks are absorbed, abandoning the schedule gradually undoes it.
do: Missed a fast or had a feast day? Just resume tomorrow. No need to start over.

claim: The same meal raises blood sugar and insulin more in the evening than in the morning.
why: Insulin sensitivity follows the body clock and is worst at night; one classic study found 25–50% higher insulin response to evening meals.
do: Make dinner lighter and earlier when you can; avoid large late-night meals.

claim: Eating your largest meal earlier in the day (breakfast or lunch) and a light dinner may help weight and blood sugar.
why: Morning insulin sensitivity is higher. In one trial, a big-breakfast group lost more weight than a big-dinner group on equal calories.
counter: A tightly controlled 2022 trial found no weight difference between big breakfast and big dinner, only less hunger with the big breakfast (Ruddick-Collins 2022 Cell Metab).

claim: Night-shift work is linked to higher rates of obesity and diabetes, partly because meals fall when the body handles food worst.
why: Eating at biological night meets low insulin sensitivity; disrupted sleep raises cortisol and appetite.
do: On night shifts, keep the main meal before the shift and avoid heavy eating overnight.

claim: Hard-training athletes and highly stressed people should introduce fasting gradually. Chronic under-eating backfires.
why: Fasting adds a stressor; combined with heavy training or life stress it can push into energy deficiency, hurting performance, sleep and hormones.

claim: The 20:4 "Warrior Diet" eats all food in a 4-hour evening window, a 20-hour daily fast.
why: A longer daily fast deepens the low-insulin period; Hofmekler pairs it with whole foods and interval training.
counter: The evening window conflicts with the circadian evidence favoring earlier eating (CGF-12-006).

claim: "You can be hungry, but you should not feel sick." Faintness, nausea or feeling unwell means stop the fast; don't push through.
why: Hunger is an expected, passing signal. Illness-like symptoms point to low blood sugar, low blood pressure or electrolyte trouble.
do: Stop, eat something gentle, and contact your doctor if symptoms don't settle quickly.

claim: A 24-hour fast runs dinner to dinner: you still eat one meal that day, so family dinners and food-requiring medications stay possible.
why: Skipping breakfast and lunch gives a full day of low insulin with minimal disruption; nutrient needs are met at the one meal.
do: Two or three 24-hour fasts a week is the common starting rhythm.

claim: The 36-hour fast skips one full day (dinner on day 1 to breakfast on day 3); add a skipped breakfast and it becomes 42 hours.
why: Fung's clinic uses 36–42 h fasts three times a week for type 2 diabetes until medications are off and weight is at target, then eases off.
counter: That schedule ran under medical supervision with frequent glucose checks.

claim: 5:2 means five normal days and two days at about 500 kcal (women) or 600 kcal (men), in one or two small meals.
why: A small allowance makes fasting days easier while still producing most of fasting's hormonal shifts; it's commonly kept as a long-term maintenance pattern.

claim: Alternate-day fasting alternates normal days with ~500–600 kcal days. It works for weight loss, but more people drop out than with daily dieting.
why: Two months of ADF cut ~5.7 kg on average. In a year-long RCT it matched daily calorie restriction for weight, with higher dropout.

claim: After a longer fast, eat normally to fullness with whole, low-sugar food. Don't add calorie restriction on top.
why: The fast already creates the deficit. Stacking deliberate calorie cuts afterward is hard to sustain and invites metabolic slowing and rebound.

claim: Waist size tells you more about metabolic health than weight. Aim to keep your waist below half your height.
why: Waist circumference reflects visceral fat around the organs, the fat most tied to diabetes and heart disease.
do: Measure at the navel once a month; log it next to your fasts.
note: Phase-2 idea: optional waist entry; pairs with plateau trigger ("scale stuck, waist shrinking?").

claim: In a 1968 hospital study, 44 of 46 people completed a 14-day fast on calorie-free drinks, with almost no hunger after day one.
why: Patients reported well-being, even euphoria. Average loss was ~7.8 kg; all three insulin-treated diabetics came off insulin. Half didn't keep to the follow-up diet at home.

claim: The longest recorded fast lasted 382 days under medical supervision: weight fell from 207 to 82 kg, and was 89 kg five years later.
why: With non-caloric fluids, vitamins and monitored supplements, his body ran on its own fat while blood sugar stayed normal.
counter: An extreme, closely supervised case, not a template. Fung says blood sugar stayed "well within normal"; the paper reports ~30 mg/dL for the last 8 months (asymptomatic), plus low magnesium and temporary high calcium (PMID 4803438).

claim: The "metabolic switch" from burning mostly glucose to mostly fat and ketones typically happens 12–36 hours after the last meal.
why: Timing depends on how full liver glycogen was. A carb-heavy dinner and inactivity push it later; low-carb eating and exercise bring it sooner.
do: A walk or workout during the fast, and a lower-carb last meal, both speed up the switch.
counter: Fung writes that ketones take 36–48 h to "ramp up"; that's when they become the brain's major fuel, but blood ketones start rising much earlier.
note: STAGE AUDIT: supports app's 12–18 h fat-burning and 18–24 h ketosis stages as "typical", if worded as variable.

claim: Expect about 0.25 kg (½ lb) of fat lost per fasting day; 45 kg of excess fat equals roughly 200 days of complete fasting.
why: Studies of long fasts show 0.2–0.35 kg/day once water is excluded, matching a steady ~2,000 kcal/day burn with no metabolic shutdown.
note: Complements CGF-05-013.

claim: Blood electrolytes stay normal in most extended fasts. Magnesium is the one that more often runs low, especially in diabetes.
why: Most magnesium sits inside cells, so blood tests underestimate stores; Fung's clinic routinely supplements it during long fasts.
do: For fasts beyond a few days, ask your doctor about magnesium; muscle cramps are a hint it may be low.

claim: Few bowel movements during a long fast are normal and usually painless. The 382-day faster went over a month between them.
why: With no food coming in, little stool forms; discomfort comes from a full colon, which a fasting colon isn't.
do: No action needed unless uncomfortable. Eat more fiber and vegetables on eating days; psyllium helps; ask your doctor if it persists.

claim: Fung's clinic rarely ends fasts at 2–3 days. Day 2 is hardest, so for supervised patients it continues to 7–14 days.
why: After day 2, hunger drops and benefits continue to build. Stopping right after the hardest point wastes the easier stretch that follows.
counter: Clinic practice with monitoring. Unsupervised fasts beyond ~3 days carry real risks (SCI-02-001, CGF-14-007).

claim: Refeeding syndrome is a rare but dangerous shift of phosphorus, magnesium and potassium when eating resumes after a long fast.
why: Food raises insulin, which pulls minerals into cells to rebuild glycogen and protein. Blood levels can crash, causing weakness, confusion, cramps or heart-rhythm problems.
do: After fasts of 5+ days, restart with small meals, and seek care for weakness, palpitations, confusion or breathlessness.

claim: Highest refeeding risk: BMI under 18.5, over 10% weight lost in 6 months, alcohol misuse, eating disorder, cancer, or bowel disease.
why: These states deplete mineral stores already, so a fast followed by refeeding can tip them into dangerous deficiency.
do: If any of these apply, don't do extended fasts; at most short fasts under 24 h, with your doctor's agreement.

claim: Keep moving during extended fasts. Normal activity and exercise help preserve muscle and bone.
why: Disuse, not fasting itself, drove much of the muscle and bone loss in David Blaine's 44-day fast in a box, where he couldn't stand or walk.
do: Walk daily and keep light strength work going; skip intense sessions if you feel faint.

claim: Ankle and foot swelling after a long fast is a known, usually temporary effect of refeeding.
why: Rising insulin makes the kidneys retain salt and water again ("refeeding edema"). It normally settles within days.
do: Keep salt moderate in the first days of eating. See a doctor if swelling is severe or comes with breathlessness.

claim: Fung's single most important tip: fit fasting into your life, not your life into fasting.
why: Adherence decides results. Forcing fasts through holidays, weddings and trips breeds resentment and quitting; flexible scheduling lasts.
do: Skip fasting on celebration days without guilt; resume your usual schedule the day after.

claim: Keep your fasting to a small circle. Tell a few supportive people, not everyone.
why: Many people discourage fasting out of unfamiliarity; a close, like-minded support group helps, while broad announcements invite pushback.

claim: Big dinner tonight? Skip breakfast and lunch. Fasting before a social meal is the easiest way to fit both.
why: Breakfast is rarely social, and lunch on workdays is easy to work through; a planned feast then lands on a day that's mostly fasted.

claim: Break a fast gently: a small snack first, then the main meal 30–60 minutes later. The longer the fast, the gentler the restart.
why: Pent-up appetite is mostly psychological; a pause lets hunger waves pass and spares a rested gut from overload and cramping.
do: After fasts under 24 h, no special care is needed. For longer ones, prepare the small dish in advance so convenience food doesn't win.

claim: Good first bites: a few nuts, a spoon of nut butter, a small salad, raw vegetables with olive oil, vegetable soup, or a little meat.
why: Small, fatty or fibrous portions satisfy without a big glucose and insulin spike, easing the gut back to work.
do: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, and drink a tall glass of water before and after.
counter: Fung's later advice (YT PVJCdREj4Og) flags nuts, seeds, nut butters, raw vegetables, eggs and dairy as the most common post-fast troublemakers; prefer YT-02-001.
note: CONFLICT with newer Fung advice; superseded by YT-02-001.

claim: If your stomach is sensitive after fasting, eggs are the most common trigger of discomfort at the first meal.
why: Fung's clinic observed eggs most often caused GI distress at refeeding; the reason isn't established.

claim: After breaking a fast, eat as if it never happened: a normal, nutritious meal, not a binge.
why: Compensating with a feast undoes the deficit and reinforces a fast-then-binge cycle.
note: Overlaps CGF-13-006 and CGF-03-010; merge at distillation.

claim: A glass of water before a meal reduces how much you eat.
why: Water stretches the stomach and dampens appetite; in a 12-week trial, pre-meal water increased weight loss in older adults.
do: Drink a full glass about 30 minutes before your first meal and before dinner.

claim: Cinnamon slows stomach emptying and may blunt both hunger and blood-sugar rises.
why: A teaspoon of cinnamon with a meal slowed gastric emptying in a small trial; it adds flavor to tea at no cost to the fast.

claim: A growling stomach often settles with sparkling mineral water.
why: The mechanism is unclear; Fung's patients report that minerals and carbonation calm stomach noise and cramping.

claim: Chia seeds soaked in water form a filling gel that can carry you through a hard stretch of a fast.
why: Their soluble fiber absorbs liquid and swells; the energy is small enough that Fung judges the trade-off worthwhile for adherence.
counter: Technically breaks the fast.

claim: Dizziness while fasting usually means low water and salt, or, if you take blood-pressure pills, pressure dropping too low.
why: Falling insulin flushes sodium and water; antihypertensives then overshoot. Standing up quickly makes it worse.
do: Drink water with a pinch of salt, rise slowly, and ask your doctor about BP medication if it recurs.

claim: Headaches in your first few fasts are common and usually temporary, often from the drop in salt intake.
why: Going from a salty diet to almost no salt changes fluid balance; the body adapts within a few fasts.
do: Take extra salt in water or drink mineral water.

claim: Mild tiredness early on is common, but persistent fatigue is not normal fasting. Stop and see your doctor.
why: Most people feel energized by rising noradrenaline. Lasting exhaustion points to dehydration, low salt, low blood sugar or another problem.

claim: Red flags that mean stop: persistent nausea, vomiting, dizziness, fatigue, very high or low blood sugar, or lethargy. Hunger and constipation are normal.
why: These signs fall outside the normal adaptation to fasting and can signal dehydration, electrolyte trouble or medication problems.
do: Stop the fast and contact your doctor.
note: Phase-2: single source for an in-app "is this normal?" symptom check.

claim: If you keep having low blood sugar on fasting days, your medication dose is too high. That's not the fasting failing.
why: Diabetes drugs are dosed for eating days. Repeated lows mean the dose needs reducing, which only your doctor should do.
do: Record the readings and times, and contact your doctor before the next fast.

claim: On blood-pressure medication, check your blood pressure at home during fasting periods.
why: Fasting lowers pressure by shedding salt and water; combined with medication, it can fall too low.

claim: High morning blood sugar during a multi-day fast isn't a failure: it's stored sugar the liver is releasing, the dawn phenomenon.
why: Before waking and during fasting, glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline and GH push liver glucose out. With insulin resistance, blood sugar shows it.
do: Look at the trend over weeks, not one reading. It eases as stored sugar is cleared.

claim: You can exercise while fasting. A 3.5-day fast didn't reduce strength, anaerobic capacity or endurance in one study.
why: Glycogen covers about a day of needs and fat supplies the rest; rising noradrenaline supports effort.
do: Keep your usual workouts; scale back if you feel faint, and expect a ~2-week dip if you're newly fat-adapting.
counter: Fung says fasting lets you "build muscle faster" via GH; there's no evidence for that. Fasting GH doesn't act as an anabolic signal.

claim: Training in a fasted state builds more fat-burning machinery in muscle.
why: Low glycogen during exercise increases fat-oxidation proteins and intramuscular fat use; useful for endurance athletes.
counter: Performance gains in competition aren't consistently shown; high-intensity work may suffer.

claim: People sometimes feel "hangry" when hungry, but expectation plays a large part. Regular fasters rarely report irritability.
why: Fung suggests people act out the irritability they expect; framing fasting as normal reduces it.
counter: Hunger is linked to anger and irritability in daily-life studies (Swami 2022 PLoS One). It's real, but usually mild and fades with practice.

claim: About two-thirds of the year's average weight gain happens in the six weeks from late November to New Year.
why: Holiday feasting concentrates the surplus; the weight often isn't lost afterward, so it accumulates year after year.
do: Plan a few fasts in early January. Feasts are fine when they're followed by fasts.
note: Phase-2: seasonal/holiday-aware nudge candidate (non-intrusive).

claim: Adjust your fasting by results and by season: shorter, more frequent fasts may suit summer, longer and less frequent ones winter.
why: Goals differ (a few kilos vs severe diabetes), and stalls mean the stimulus needs to change. Nothing about the schedule is fixed.

claim: Flavor fasting water with lemon, lime, fruit slices (not eaten), vinegar, a pinch of salt, or a spoon of chia or ground flax.
why: These add taste, salt or fiber with negligible energy. Sweetened powders and drops, even sugar-free, are out.

claim: Herbal teas are unlimited while fasting. Peppermint eases gas and bloating; cinnamon chai can curb sweet cravings.
why: Herbal infusions add warmth, ritual and flavor with no energy, so they suit any hour of the fasting day.

claim: Bitter melon tea, cinnamon and black or oolong teas are traditionally used to lower blood sugar. Take care if you're on diabetes drugs.
why: Their glucose-lowering effect adds to medication's, raising the risk of lows during a fast.
do: On insulin or diabetes pills, check with your doctor before using bitter melon regularly.
counter: Human evidence for most of these is weak; bitter melon has the most data, with modest effects.

claim: Fung's 24-hour protocol: three dinner-to-dinner (or lunch-to-lunch) fasts a week, plus a daily 16:8 on other days. It suits steady weight loss.
why: A meal every day keeps medications and family dinners possible; two fasts a week works for a gentler pace.

claim: Fung's 36-hour protocol: three full non-eating days a week (dinner to breakfast two days later). Stronger for weight and prediabetes than the 24-hour plan.
why: Longer daily stretches of low insulin lower blood sugar more; some people find a full day off food simpler than one meal.

claim: Fung's 42-hour protocol, for type 2 diabetes: three full fasting days a week plus no breakfast on any day (dinner to lunch two days later).
why: The extra hours give blood glucose and insulin more time to fall. Medication must be adjusted beforehand to avoid lows.

claim: 7–14-day fasts are a supervised clinical protocol: physician oversight, adjusted medication, a daily multivitamin, and blood tests.
why: Fung uses them for severe diabetes or obesity, limited to once a month (7 days) or every six weeks (14 days) because of refeeding risk.
do: Don't attempt fasts beyond ~3 days without your doctor's involvement.

claim: After a meal, blood sugar peaks within about an hour and insulin rises with it. While insulin is high, fat burning is paused.
why: Insulin moves incoming glucose into cells and stores the surplus as glycogen and fat, and it shuts off fat release from fat cells until levels fall.

claim: A 10–15 minute easy walk after eating noticeably lowers the blood-sugar and insulin spike from that meal.
why: Working muscles take up glucose without needing much insulin. In a meta-analysis of crossover trials, light walking cut the post-meal rise more than standing.
do: Walk after your biggest meal, especially one with bread, rice, pasta or dessert.

claim: Ravenous 3–4 hours after a sugary or starchy meal? That's often a blood-sugar rebound, not a real shortage of fuel.
why: A fast glucose spike calls up a big insulin surge that can overshoot, pushing glucose below baseline a few hours later and triggering hunger.
do: Ride it out with water or tea; next time eat protein and vegetables first and carbs last.

claim: Ghrelin, the hunger hormone, rises before your usual mealtimes and then falls whether you eat or not. Hunger at noon is partly a clock signal.
why: In people eating on a schedule, ghrelin climbed in the hour before each habitual meal and fell afterward: a learned, anticipatory pattern.

claim: A few hours after a meal (roughly 3–5, longer with insulin resistance), insulin settles back to baseline and fat cells start releasing fat again.
why: With insulin low, the brake on fat release lifts; the liver begins drawing on glycogen. A snack now raises insulin again and pushes this switch back.
do: Let this window happen: no snacks between meals.

claim: Weight-loss drugs like semaglutide or tirzepatide work; fasting on top needs care: protein, strength training and fluids matter more, not longer fasts.
why: These drugs already cut appetite steeply, so muscle loss and dehydration (from nausea or vomiting) become the risks. With insulin or sulfonylureas, lows become likelier.
do: Plan fasting with your prescriber. Make every meal protein-first, lift 2–3×/week, drink enough.
src: Ramadan GLP-1RA systematic review 2025 World J Methodol (PMID 40900863)
counter: In Ramadan studies GLP-1 drugs caused fewer lows than other diabetes drugs but more gastrointestinal effects.

claim: A year after stopping semaglutide, people had regained about two-thirds of the weight they'd lost.
why: The drug suppresses appetite only while it's taken. When it stops, hunger and the body's defended weight return unless habits have changed.
do: If you use one of these drugs, use the time to build your eating rhythm (meals, no snacks, fasting days) for when you stop.
src: Wilding 2022 Diabetes Obes Metab (STEP 1 extension, PMID 35441470)

claim: On lithium, dehydration or a sudden drop in salt intake can raise lithium to toxic levels. Fasting needs your psychiatrist's agreement and good hydration.
why: The kidneys handle lithium like sodium; when salt and water fall, they retain lithium. A Ramadan study found levels stayed stable in well-controlled patients.

claim: If you take steroid replacement (adrenal insufficiency) or long-term prednisone, don't fast without your endocrinologist, and never skip a dose.
why: Without enough cortisol the body can't keep blood sugar and blood pressure up during a fast; adrenal crisis is a real risk.

claim: On warfarin, big changes in eating (fasting, far more or fewer greens) can shift your INR. Check it more often when you start.
why: Warfarin's effect depends on steady vitamin K intake and on liver metabolism; abrupt dietary change alters both.

claim: Morning fasting suits levothyroxine (thyroid hormone): it's absorbed best on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before food.
why: Food, calcium and iron all reduce absorption; a long fasted morning makes consistent dosing easier.

claim: Had kidney stones? Fasting and ketosis raise uric acid and concentrate urine; ~6% on long-term ketogenic diets developed stones, mostly uric acid.
why: Ketones compete with uric acid for excretion, and low fluid intake concentrates the urine, both favoring stone formation.
do: Drink well (pale urine), and talk to your doctor about longer fasts if you've had stones.

claim: Over 65, weight loss takes muscle and bone unless you protect them: shorter fasts, protein every meal, strength training, stand up slowly.
why: Older muscle responds less to protein, and dieting older adults lose lean mass and bone; adding resistance plus aerobic exercise preserved them in an RCT.

claim: After breaking a diet rule, people often abandon restraint entirely and eat far more: the "what-the-hell" effect.
why: Rigid all-or-nothing rules turn one slip into a perceived total failure. Restrained eaters overeat more after a "forbidden" preload than unrestrained eaters.
do: A slip is one meal, not a broken day. Resume at the next planned point.

claim: Being kind to yourself after a lapse reduces later overeating; self-criticism increases it.
why: Guilt and shame are aversive states people escape by eating. Self-compassion lowers the distress without excusing the behavior.
src: Adams & Leary 2007 J Soc Clin Psychol
counter: Single laboratory study in restrictive eaters; replications are mixed but consistent in direction.

claim: "Urge surfing" (noticing a craving's body sensations and letting it crest and pass without acting) weakened the link between craving and acting on it.
why: A craving is a time-limited wave; observing it non-judgmentally breaks the automatic craving-to-action chain. Shown in a mindfulness trial with smokers.
do: When a craving hits, name where you feel it, breathe slowly, and watch it peak and fade.
counter: Tested for smoking, not food; mechanisms are shared, food-specific evidence is smaller.

claim: Thinking about a food's long-term consequences reduces how much you crave it and engages the brain's prefrontal control regions.
