why: Cognitive reappraisal ("later" framing) recruits prefrontal cortex and dampens reward-region activity to the craved cue.
do: Before an unplanned bite, picture how you'll feel in two hours, and tomorrow.
src: Kober 2010 Proc Natl Acad Sci USA (PMID 20679212)

claim: How strongly you react to food cues (sight, smell, ads) predicts how much you eat and later weight gain.
why: Cue-induced craving is a measurable, robust driver of eating across dozens of studies, so reducing exposure is a legitimate strategy, not weakness.

claim: Craving ("wanting") and enjoyment ("liking") run on different brain systems. The urge can far exceed the pleasure the food actually gives.
why: Dopamine drives anticipation and pursuit; separate opioid "hotspots" generate pleasure. Cues can inflate wanting without increasing liking.

claim: People eat substantially more when eating with others than alone; the effect is strongest among friends and family.
why: Shared meals lengthen eating and set social norms for portions. A meta-analysis found reliable social facilitation of intake.
do: Plan fasts around social meals rather than fighting them; decide your portion before you sit down.

claim: New weeks, months, birthdays and holidays boost motivation to start fresh: the "fresh start" effect.
why: Temporal landmarks create a mental break from past failures, making a new beginning feel credible.
do: Use a landmark to restart, but don't wait for one: tomorrow is a landmark too.

claim: Effort rises as a goal gets closer (the goal-gradient effect), so near milestones keep you going better than one distant finish line.
why: Perceived progress toward a near target increases motivation; long goals feel abstract until broken into visible steps.
do: Aim for the next milestone on the dial, not the end of the fast.

claim: One night of poor sleep makes junk food more desirable: brain control regions quiet down while reward regions light up.
why: Sleep deprivation reduces frontal-cortex activity in appetite evaluation and amplifies amygdala responses to high-calorie foods.

claim: Much "hunger" is boredom. People eat to escape the empty feeling of being bored, especially when the food is a distraction.
why: Eating gives quick stimulation and shifts attention away from an aversive state of low engagement.
do: Ask "am I hungry or under-stimulated?" A task, a walk or a conversation often answers it.

claim: Many people report better mood, calm and alertness after the first days of a fast, and early clinical studies point the same way.
why: Proposed mechanisms include ketones as brain fuel, rising BDNF and noradrenaline, and changes in serotonin signaling.
counter: Mostly small, uncontrolled studies; expectation effects are large. People with mood disorders should fast only with their clinician.

claim: Every fast you complete builds confidence that you can do the next one. Mastery experience is the strongest source of self-efficacy.
why: Self-efficacy grows most from personal success, not persuasion; it predicts whether people keep a new behavior.
do: Start with fasts you can finish, then stretch. Counting completed fasts is more useful than counting failures.

claim: Around 2–3 days into a fast, muscles temporarily become less responsive to insulin. This is normal: it saves glucose for the brain.
why: Fat released from stores floods muscle and blocks insulin's glucose uptake. The effect reverses within a day or two of eating.
do: A higher-than-usual glucose reading after a multi-day fast, or right after refeeding, is expected; judge insulin health between fasts.
counter: n=12 healthy men, 60 h fast. Repeated fasting with fat loss improves insulin sensitivity over weeks, which is the long-term effect Fung describes.
note: Corrects the app's 54–72 h "insulin sensitivity resets" copy (AUDIT #4).

claim: Fung's current five-stage timeline: feeding 0–4 h, post-absorptive 4–16 h, gluconeogenesis 16–30 h, ketosis after ~2 days, protein conservation after ~6–7 days.
why: Adapted from Cahill: each stage is defined by where blood glucose comes from (food, liver glycogen, new glucose, then mostly fat and ketones).
counter: Differs from his 2016 book timeline (CGF-01-006) and from tracer data (Rothman 1991: gluconeogenesis is substantial before 16 h). Boundaries are fuzzy and individual.
note: STAGE AUDIT input. Any app timeline should say "typical" and avoid false precision.

claim: The deepest drop in hunger comes after about a week of fasting, when ghrelin falls and the body feeds almost entirely on its own fat.
why: In the protein-conservation phase, fat and ketones supply nearly all energy. That's how hunger strikers and 30–60-day fasters report little hunger.

claim: Fung claims fasting causes less loose skin after weight loss, because autophagy breaks down excess skin and connective tissue protein.
why: His reasoning: weight loss leaves surplus structural protein, and fasting-driven recycling removes what's no longer needed.
counter: No study has measured loose skin after fasting versus other weight-loss methods. Plausible mechanism, no outcome data.
note: Popular claim; keep out of the app unless evidence appears.

claim: The easiest fasts to sustain are short and frequent (16:8, one meal a day); skipping dinner is the socially hardest step.
why: Breakfast and lunch can be skipped unnoticed. A 36-hour fast removes dinner, the main family and social meal, which makes it harder to keep up week after week.
do: Build your routine around 16:8 or one meal a day; slot longer fasts into quiet periods, like when you're home alone or travelling for work.

claim: Your fasting rhythm can differ by day: longer fasts on weekdays, shorter ones on weekends with family.
why: Busy workdays make fasting easy and family weekends make it hard. Matching the fast to the day keeps the habit alive.
note: Phase-2: per-weekday default fast targets?

claim: A 36-hour fast spans two nights of sleep, so roughly 16 of its hours pass while you sleep.
why: Starting after dinner and ending at breakfast two days later puts two full sleeping periods inside the fast.

claim: Fung advises keeping dry fasts (no water) under about 16–18 hours.
why: Without fluids you dehydrate alongside fasting, which limits safe duration. Some find short dry fasts ease hunger and frequent urination.
do: For religious dry fasts, keep them within a day, rehydrate well afterwards, and avoid them if you're on diuretics or have kidney problems.
note: Complements CGF-01-020; relevant to nirjala Ekadashi fasts in the lunar feature.

claim: A small slip, like a splash of cream, a few nuts or a bite of salad, doesn't reset your fast to zero. Just continue.
why: A tiny intake briefly bumps insulin, which falls again within a short time, so fat-burning soon resumes. The hours before still count.
do: Don't restart the timer for a nibble; note it if you like and carry on.
note: Phase-2 UX: never force a timer reset for small slips; non-punitive framing.

claim: Vitamins, vitamin D, fish oil and electrolytes can be taken during a fast; they don't meaningfully raise insulin.
why: They carry negligible energy. They aren't required for short fasts, since you'll eat again soon, but they don't break the fast.

claim: If you feel lightheaded while fasting, a pinch of salt under the tongue or in water often helps within minutes.
why: With no food you take in almost no sodium; a small dose restores blood volume and pressure.
do: Sit down, take the salt with water, and stop the fast if dizziness persists or you're on blood-pressure medication.

claim: When the scale stalls, take a weekly photo or measure your waist. Body shape often changes before weight does.
why: Water shifts mask fat loss on the scale for weeks; photos and waist size reveal progress that the number hides.

claim: The most common fasting mistake is eating too much when you eat: fitting a whole day's food, or junk food, into one meal or window.
why: The fast works by letting stored fat cover the missing meals. If the next meal replaces all of them, there's no deficit left to cover.
do: Eat a normal-sized, whole-food meal after a fast; slightly larger is fine, but not three meals in one sitting.
counter: Fung attributes null RCT results (Trepanowski 2017, Lowe 2020) to this design flaw. But in Liu 2022, with calories matched, time-restricted eating added no benefit over calorie restriction.

claim: In 30–60-day fasts, researchers drove blood sugar extremely low with insulin, and the fasters felt nothing, because ketones were fueling their brains.
why: After weeks of fasting the brain runs mostly on ketones, so glucose levels that would cause seizures in a fed person went unnoticed.
counter: Experimental, under hospital supervision. It shows ketones' protective role and should never be tested at home.
note: VERIFIED citation.

claim: After fasts over 24 hours, have a small "pre-meal" 30 minutes before the main meal: a little fish or meat, cooked vegetables, or avocado.
why: Digestion slows during a fast. A small, easy first portion wakes it gently and takes the edge off appetite before the full meal.
do: Prefer cooked over raw vegetables at first; a glass of water with soaked chia also works.
note: Canonical break-fast food card; supersedes CGF-15-005 food list.

claim: Foods most likely to upset your stomach right after a fast: nuts and seeds, nut butters, raw or fibrous vegetables, eggs, dairy, wine.
why: They take more stomach acid and enzymes to digest, which are slow to return after a fast. Tolerance varies by person.

claim: After a fast, psychological hunger usually far exceeds physical hunger. That gap is why people overeat and end up bloated or nauseous.
why: Having gone without, the mind demands a feast while the stomach and enzymes are only just restarting.
do: Serve a normal portion, eat slowly, and wait before deciding on seconds.

claim: Avoid sweeteners toward the end of a fast. They sharpen the urge to eat and make overeating at the first meal more likely.
why: Sweet taste primes appetite without satisfying it, amplifying the psychological hunger that peaks at refeeding.

claim: Refeeding risk also involves thiamine (vitamin B1). Long-term antacid or diuretic users, elderly people eating poorly, and patients recovering from surgery face extra risk.
why: Magnesium or aluminium antacids bind phosphorus; diuretics drain potassium and magnesium. Refeeding then pulls these minerals into cells, so blood levels crash further.
do: On diuretics or daily antacids, don't do multi-day fasts without your doctor checking your blood levels.

claim: Body-fat scales and DEXA scans often report "muscle loss" during fasting that is really water and glycogen loss.
why: Bioimpedance and DEXA estimate lean mass assuming a stable body-water content. Fasting sheds water, which these methods read as lost lean tissue, and it returns when you eat.
do: Track strength or a tape measure rather than a smart scale's muscle reading during fasting periods.

claim: In a 10-day medically supervised fast (~250 kcal/day), grip strength held steady and leg strength rose, while hunger dropped over the first five days.
why: Stair-climb times were unchanged during the fast and improved after refeeding. Noradrenaline likely boosts muscle performance short term.
counter: Small, healthy men; some lean tissue was lost. The study shows function is preserved, not zero protein loss.
note: VERIFIED citation.

claim: Fung argues most people need far less protein than popular advice suggests, and that much of extra protein simply becomes glucose.
why: His view: the body recycles most amino acids from its own protein turnover, so daily net losses are small and excess intake is converted for fuel.
counter: Isotope studies show dietary protein contributes little to glucose production (Fromentin 2013 Diabetes). During weight loss, ~1.2–1.6 g/kg protein helps preserve lean mass.
note: Conflicts with CGF-03-005 (keep that).

claim: In a 2024 randomized trial, heart-attack patients who did intermittent fasting recovered more heart pumping function than those on a regular diet.
why: INTERFAST-MI: 48 patients after a major heart attack; ejection fraction improved more with fasting at 4 weeks. Fung cites it as evidence fasting doesn't erode heart muscle.
counter: Small single-center pilot, not blinded. Heart patients should fast only with their cardiologist's approval.
note: VERIFIED citation (abstract).

claim: Autophagy comes in specialized forms: clearing fat droplets, protein clumps, microbes and worn-out mitochondria. Too little and too much are both harmful.
why: These sub-types (lipophagy, aggrephagy, xenophagy, mitophagy) link autophagy to metabolic, neurological, infectious and vascular disease in research.
counter: Mechanistic and disease-association research; it doesn't show what a given fast does in a given person.

claim: The best time to train is toward the end of a fast, then eat a protein-rich meal afterward.
why: Late in a fast noradrenaline is high and fat-burning is running; the meal after training supplies building material when muscle is primed to rebuild.
do: Example: fast from dinner, train at noon the next day, break the fast with lunch.

claim: Do everything you normally do while fasting: work, walk, run, lift. Fasting doesn't require resting.
why: Stored fat holds 100,000+ kcal; the body draws on it as needed, and fasting hormones activate rather than sedate.
note: Overlaps CGF-15-020 and CGF-14-010; merge at distillation.

claim: Keeping weight off is harder than losing it; an accountability partner or coach greatly improves maintenance.
why: Someone to report to keeps habits going after motivation fades, which is when most regain happens.

claim: Design out hunger triggers: don't work at the kitchen table, batch-cook on eating days, and order groceries online on fasting days.
why: The kitchen, cooking smells and grocery aisles fire conditioned hunger repeatedly. Avoiding them saves willpower for when it's really needed.

claim: Schedule something engaging at your usual mealtime, like a walk with a friend, a call or a bath. The hunger wave passes while you're busy.
why: Hunger waves last roughly 30–45 minutes. Planned activity at the predictable peak means the wave passes without a decision being needed.
note: Phase-2: optional "usual mealtime" nudge with a suggested activity, user-controlled.

claim: Make "no snacks" your default rather than a daily decision. A new eating habit feels strange at first, then becomes automatic.
why: Defaults cost no willpower. Fung says a new habit settles in about two weeks; studies find habits take anywhere from weeks to months.
counter: In Lally 2010 the median time to automaticity was ~66 days (range 18–254). Expect weeks, not days.

claim: Bitter drinks such as unsweetened herbal or turmeric teas, or green tea, can dampen appetite during a hunger wave.
why: Bitterness tends to turn the palate away from food; green tea's EGCG may have a mild appetite-suppressing effect.

claim: Headaches and dizziness in early fasting usually fade within about two weeks of regular fasting.
why: The body adapts to lower salt intake and to fuel switching; until then, extra salt (salted water, sugar-free pickle juice) relieves most symptoms.

claim: Some people get loose stools early in fasting as the body sheds water. It usually settles within days.
why: Falling insulin releases retained water; some leaves through the bowel rather than the kidneys.
do: Psyllium husk in water can firm things up; persistent diarrhea or signs of dehydration mean stop and seek advice.

claim: Trouble sleeping or waking early on fasting days is common, a side effect of the energizing hormones fasting releases.
why: Noradrenaline rises during fasting, so you may feel alert at bedtime. Fung frames it as extra energy, not a problem.
do: Don't force sleep: wind down without screens, try a warm (Epsom) bath, go to bed when tired. If insomnia persists, shorten or move your fasts.

claim: Fung suggests lemon juice or diluted apple-cider vinegar for fasting heartburn; antacids if needed, and shorter fasts if it persists.
why: His view is that mild acid prompts the stomach to empty forward. Losing weight reduces reflux over time.
counter: Acidic drinks worsen reflux for many people; standard advice avoids them. Test cautiously.

claim: Fasting is easier when eating days stay consistent: weekend junk food makes weekday fasts harder to restart.
why: Big swings in carbohydrate intake keep refilling glycogen and resetting cravings, so each fast has to re-adapt.

claim: Fung argues the case for low-salt diets is weaker than taught: average blood-pressure drops are small and partly inflated by publication bias.
why: He cites a 34-trial meta-analysis (−5.4/−2.4 mmHg), funnel-plot asymmetry, a 2015 Intersalt reanalysis without four isolated tribes, and a 2013 Institute of Medicine report.
counter: Salt reduction lowers blood pressure most in people with hypertension, and lower intake cut cardiovascular events in a large RCT (SSaSS, Neal 2021 N Engl J Med). Japan's high salt intake went with very high stroke rates.
note: Don't ship general "salt is fine" claims. Salt during fasting (CGF-00-008, YT-01-011) is a separate, defensible context.

claim: Most people eat less magnesium than recommended. Refining strips most of it: white flour loses ~80% of wheat's magnesium, polished rice ~80%, cornstarch ~97%.
why: Whole grains, nuts, legumes, dark chocolate, tofu and seafood are rich sources. Processing, softened water, alcohol, diuretics and gut disease all lower intake or raise losses.
counter: In US surveys about half of adults fall below the average requirement. Fung's 50–85% is the upper range; soil-depletion claims are contested.

claim: If you supplement magnesium, choose citrate or glycinate; magnesium oxide is poorly absorbed and mostly acts as a laxative.
why: Organic magnesium salts are absorbed several times better; oxide carries a lot of elemental magnesium but little enters the blood.
do: With kidney disease, don't take magnesium supplements without your doctor: impaired kidneys can't clear the excess.
note: Fung also lists carbonate among the "organic" forms; it's inorganic. Omit it.

claim: Muscle cramps, twitches, constipation and fatigue can signal low magnesium, even when blood tests look normal.
why: Only about 1% of the body's magnesium is in the blood; most is in bone and muscle, so a blood test can miss a deficit.

claim: Eat carbohydrates last. Same meal, carbs eaten after protein and vegetables: blood sugar and insulin rose roughly 40–50% less.
why: Protein, fat and fiber eaten first slow stomach emptying and prime gut hormones, so starch arrives later and gentler.
do: Start with protein and vegetables; leave bread, rice or potato for the end, ideally 10 minutes later. Ask restaurants to bring bread with the meal.
counter: Small crossover studies (n≈11–16); long-term outcome data are lacking.
note: VERIFIED: prediabetes study, glucose peaks >40% lower, iAUC −38.8% with protein/vegetables first.

claim: Eating carbs first can cause a sugar crash a few hours later: in one study a prediabetic participant became shaky and sweaty.
why: A fast glucose spike triggers a large insulin surge that overshoots, dropping blood sugar below baseline around three hours after eating.

claim: Adding acid to starch blunts its blood-sugar spike: vinegar, lemon juice, or pickled and fermented foods alongside bread or rice.
why: Acid inactivates saliva's starch-digesting enzyme, which does much of the work in the stomach. Vinegar with bread lowered glucose and insulin dose-dependently and increased fullness.
do: Avoid "naked carbs": pair starch with vinegar dressing, pickles, lemon, protein or fat.

claim: Plateau checklist beyond diet: cut all sweeteners, sleep enough, and actively manage stress.
why: Sweeteners keep cravings alive; short sleep increases appetite and intake; chronic stress raises cortisol, which promotes weight gain and stress eating.
do: Treat sleep and stress like part of the protocol: regular bedtime, daily movement, meditation, yoga or time with people.
src: Al Khatib 2017 Eur J Clin Nutr

claim: Short sleep makes people eat roughly 250–400 kcal more the next day.
why: Sleep loss raises hunger and reward responses to food and weakens self-control, and it reduces insulin sensitivity.
src: Al Khatib 2017 Eur J Clin Nutr

claim: "Make hunger your friend." Reframe hunger during a fast as a sign you're on track, not a warning.
why: Hunger will show up physically and psychologically; treating it as an expected companion lowers anxiety and the urge to bolt.
note: Phase-2 copy candidate (reframing, not instruction).

claim: Your body defends a set weight. Overfed people burned ~500 kcal/day more; after losing 10%, they burned 300–400 kcal/day less.
why: Like a thermostat, the body adjusts energy use to resist change in either direction. This is why calorie cutting alone tends to stall.
counter: Fung's view that insulin sets the "thermostat" is a hypothesis. Leptin and brain circuits are the best-established regulators.

claim: In type 1 diabetes, higher insulin doses caused substantially more weight gain over years. Insulin dose and weight move together.
why: In the DCCT trial, intensive insulin therapy led to significant weight gain in about 30% of patients over ~9 years.

claim: Many "breakfast foods" are dessert in disguise: cereals, muffins, pastries, fruit-on-the-bottom yogurt, breakfast bars, jam on white toast.
why: Low-fat breakfast products often replaced fat with sugar. Refined carbs spike glucose and insulin, leaving you ravenous by mid-morning.
do: If you eat breakfast, choose eggs, meat, plain yogurt or slow-cooked whole oats, or simply delay your first meal.

claim: Sugar (sucrose, high-fructose corn syrup) is worse than starch. Its fructose half is processed by the liver, where excess becomes liver fat.
why: Unlike glucose, fructose bypasses most cells and is converted to fat in the liver when intake is high, driving fatty liver and insulin resistance.

claim: Breakfast can wait. Around 4–5 a.m. your body releases hormones that put fuel into the blood, so you're already fueled when you wake.
why: Growth hormone, cortisol and noradrenaline mobilize stored energy before waking; that's why morning hunger is typically lowest.
do: Eat when you're hungry, not because it's morning. 7 a.m., 9 a.m. or noon all work.
note: Overlaps CGF-09-002 and CGF-01-015; merge at distillation.

claim: Fatty liver affects roughly a quarter to a third of adults, mostly without symptoms. It's driven largely by sugar and refined starch, not dietary fat.
why: The liver turns excess glucose and especially fructose into new fat (de novo lipogenesis). In overfeeding studies, a 2% weight gain came with ~27% more liver fat.

claim: Liver fat responds fast. Teenage boys who cut added sugar to under 3% of calories reduced liver fat by about a third in 8 weeks.
why: Removing fructose shuts down much of the liver's new-fat production; the stored fat is then exported and burned.

claim: In a randomized trial, both 5:2 fasting and a low-carb diet more than halved liver fat in people with fatty liver over 12 weeks.
why: Both cut the insulin and sugar load that drives liver fat production. The standard-advice group improved far less.
note: VERIFIED citation.

claim: With kidney disease, fast only under your nephrologist. Early diabetic kidney damage may improve with periodic fasting, but electrolyte and medication risks are higher.
why: In a 6-month trial, monthly 5-day fasting-mimicking cycles lowered HbA1c and insulin resistance and reduced urine protein in early disease.
do: If you have kidney disease or protein in your urine, bring a fasting plan to your kidney doctor rather than starting alone.
counter: Proof-of-concept, n=40; the overall urine-protein result wasn't statistically significant.

claim: Skipping breakfast is the easiest fast; skipping dinner is the most effective.
why: Breakfast is small (~20% of daily intake), little-hungry and rarely social. Dinner is the biggest meal, eaten when insulin responses run highest, but it's the hardest to skip.
do: Default to skipping breakfast; swap in a skipped dinner when you want a stronger effect, such as before an event.

claim: Quick hunger fixes from Fung: green tea, a little salt in water, diluted apple-cider vinegar, or chia seeds soaked in water.
why: Each fills the stomach, adds ritual or dulls appetite at near-zero energy cost, bridging the 30–45 minutes a hunger wave lasts.

claim: Women's appetite shifts with the cycle: lower in the first half (rising estrogen), higher after ovulation (progesterone). Plan longer fasts for the first two weeks.
why: Estrogen suppresses appetite and progesterone stimulates it; food intake measurably dips around ovulation and rises in the luteal phase.
do: Do longer fasts in days ~1–14; in the week or two before your period, favor shorter fasts or a simple eating window.
note: Phase-2 idea: optional cycle-aware fasting suggestion (opt-in only, privacy-sensitive).

claim: Many women find a single 3-day fast easier than alternating fast and eating days throughout the week.
why: Once past day 2, hunger tends to fade. Repeated restarts mean repeatedly facing the hardest early hours.
counter: Clinical experience. Multi-day fasts carry more risk if you're on medication.

claim: Vary your one-meal-a-day meal: lunch one day, dinner the next. That alternates ~30-hour and ~16-hour fasts.
why: Megan Ramos reports that varying the meal time breaks stalls, especially for women, while keeping the simplicity of one meal a day.

claim: In the years before menopause, women gain roughly 0.5 kg a year and lose lean mass. It's a hormonal shift, not a failure of discipline.
why: Falling estrogen raises appetite and moves fat from hips toward the belly (visceral fat); poor sleep, common in perimenopause, speeds the gain.
do: Prioritize strength training, protein and sleep; fasting helps, but expect slower progress during this window.

claim: Women lose weight with intermittent fasting at about the same rate as men; women-only RCTs show it works at least as well as daily dieting.
why: Harvie's 2011 and 2013 trials (women only) and mixed-sex trials found no meaningful sex difference in weight-loss rate.
note: Overlaps CGF-10-008.

claim: Protein, fat and fiber trigger your gut's own fullness hormones (GLP-1, GIP), the same pathway Ozempic-type drugs amplify.
why: These nutrients slow stomach emptying and stimulate incretin release; fiber feeds gut bacteria whose fatty acids boost GLP-1 further.
do: Build meals around protein, natural fats and fibrous vegetables to stay full longer.
counter: Natural GLP-1 rises are far smaller and shorter than drug levels; don't expect drug-like effects.

claim: Bitter melon and curcumin (turmeric) may raise GLP-1 and lower blood sugar, which may explain their traditional use for diabetes.
why: Bitter-taste receptors in the gut may trigger incretin release; studies of bitter gourd show glucose-lowering effects.
counter: Small and animal studies. On diabetes medication these can add to the risk of lows (CGF-16-004).

claim: Large weight loss tends to remove visceral (organ) fat proportionally faster than fat under the skin, which is the metabolically important part.
why: In a 12-week 600-kcal/day diet, visceral fat fell roughly twice as much in proportion as body weight; time-restricted eating plus low-carb cut visceral fat in an RCT.
counter: Fung claims fasting prevents "Ozempic face". Facial fat loss follows any rapid, large weight loss, and his evidence is photos.

claim: Fung claims fasting avoids the hollow-cheeked "Ozempic face" and loose skin, through growth hormone, autophagy and preferential visceral-fat loss.
why: His argument rests on mechanisms and before/after photos of patients versus celebrities on GLP-1 drugs.
counter: No comparative study exists. Speed and amount of weight loss, age and genetics likely dominate.

claim: Snacking became near-universal (97% of Americans by 2006) and snacks' share of daily calories grew. Most snacks are salty foods and desserts.
why: Meals barely shrink to compensate, so snacks add energy; they're mostly shelf-stable, ultra-processed foods rather than fruit, vegetables or protein.

claim: Snacks work like appetizers: small tasty bites that stoke appetite and keep food on your mind all day.
why: Each snack restarts insulin and the cephalic response; frequent eating also means more thinking about food.
do: Treat "no snacks" as the first and most powerful fasting step. If you're not hungry, don't eat.

claim: Skipping breakfast doesn't make you eat more overall. In trials, breakfast eaters consumed ~260 kcal more per day and weren't lighter.
why: The meal after a skipped breakfast grows only slightly; total daily intake falls. A meta-analysis of RCTs found no weight benefit from eating breakfast.

claim: IGF-1, a growth signal linked to cancer and aging, follows a U-shaped curve: both very high and very low levels are linked to higher mortality.
why: High IGF-1 drives cell growth (associated with several cancers); very low levels reflect malnutrition. Dairy and animal protein raise it most.
counter: Observational associations; causation and optimal ranges are unsettled.

claim: Ordinary daily fasting barely moves IGF-1. It falls when intake drops below about half of normal, as on full fast days or multi-day fasts.
why: A meta-analysis found IGF-1 decreased only in fasting regimens with severe calorie restriction; occasional full fast days (as in many religions) supply that dip.
counter: Fung's figures for this meta-analysis are unverified.
note: UNVERIFIED: PubMed search found no matching IF/IGF-1 meta-analysis; keep tail until located.

claim: Sleeping about an hour more cut food intake by ~270 kcal a day in short sleepers, and they lost weight without any diet advice.
why: In a 2022 RCT, adults sleeping under 6.5 h extended sleep by ~1.2 h; intake fell while energy expenditure didn't change.
do: If you sleep under 6.5 hours, an earlier bedtime may be the easiest weight lever you have.

claim: Eating out of sync with your body clock raises the blood sugar and insulin response to the same meal and lowers leptin, the fullness hormone.
why: In circadian-misalignment experiments, identical meals produced higher glucose and insulin, and lower leptin, which means more hunger and more storage.
src: Scheer 2009 Proc Natl Acad Sci USA
note: Supports CGF-12-006 and CGF-12-008.

claim: Eat a simple home-cooked meal, low in sugar and starch, the night before a fast. Restaurant meals make the next day harder.
why: Sugar and starch make you retain water; when insulin falls you shed it quickly, losing electrolytes, which causes headache, nausea and fatigue.

claim: Set a reminder every couple of hours on fasting days to drink: water with a pinch of salt or pickle juice.
why: Most of our water and electrolytes normally come with food; new fasters lose extra fluid as insulin drops, and it's easy to forget to drink.
note: Phase-2: optional hydration nudges during a fast (off by default; respect non-intrusiveness).

claim: Megan Ramos recommends an Epsom-salt bath or foot soak the night before a fast to top up magnesium and calm fasting jitters.
why: Her view: noradrenaline rises during fasting and magnesium counters the wired feeling; she considers skin absorption better than pills for people with gut issues.
counter: Fung says oral citrate or glycinate is better studied and skin absorption is uncertain (YT lbZz1yCdA8U; Gröber 2017 Nutrients). The bath relaxes either way.
note: CONFLICT between Fung and Ramos; ship as "relaxing ritual", not as a magnesium source.

claim: Getting back on track after a break or a stressful period: start with three meals and no snacks, then drop meals one at a time.
why: Removing snacks lowers insulin with almost no hunger cost; regaining appetite control first makes the return to longer fasts easier.
note: Phase-2: "restart" path after a long gap in the log.

claim: If stress makes you eat, choose natural fats and protein (olives, avocado, eggs, fatty meat) over chips and sweets.
why: Fat and protein satisfy without blood-sugar swings; processed carbs bring water retention, brain fog, poor sleep and higher sugars that last for days.
do: Before eating, ask yourself what this food will do to you in a few hours.

claim: Keep your eating window short: a meal that stretches into hours of grazing is snacking in disguise. Ramos's group challenge capped meals at 90 minutes.
why: Grazing repeatedly raises insulin; a defined start and end keeps the fasted hours truly fasted.

claim: PCOS is the most common hormonal disorder in women of reproductive age, and insulin resistance drives it, including in lean women.
why: High insulin pushes the ovaries to make excess androgens and disrupts ovulation. Diagnosis needs two of three: androgen signs, polycystic ovaries, irregular or absent cycles.
do: Irregular cycles, acne or excess hair with weight gain around the middle? Ask your doctor about PCOS and insulin resistance.
src: Brito Pateguana & Fung 2020 The PCOS Plan
counter: Prevalence is ~6–13% by standard criteria; the 10–30% quoted is higher than most estimates.

claim: Starting fasting can shift your cycle for the first few months. Occasional delays are common; months without a period are not.
why: Any big change in diet, weight or stress can move ovulation. Fasting Method coaches report cycles usually settle within 3–4 months.
do: Track your cycle. If periods stop for 3 months or more (and you're not pregnant), stop fasting and see your doctor.
note: Refines CGF-10-009 (stop on amenorrhea) with the normal-variation nuance.

claim: Women's weight loss runs in a monthly wave, not a straight line. Compare your weight at the same point in each cycle.
why: Water retention rises in the second half of the cycle and drops after menstruation, so week-to-week changes mislead.

claim: Pateguana says up to 80% of women at fertility clinics have PCOS; reversing insulin resistance often restores ovulation.
why: PCOS-driven anovulation is the leading treatable cause of female infertility; weight loss and lower insulin restore ovulation in many.
counter: PCOS causes ~70–80% of anovulatory infertility, not 80% of all fertility-clinic patients. Trying to conceive is itself a reason to involve your doctor before fasting.

claim: After menopause women lose their cardiovascular head start, and heart-disease risk climbs toward men's.
why: Estrogen protects blood vessels and insulin sensitivity; its loss raises visceral fat, lipids and risk.

claim: There's no point eating fat you're not hungry for. "Fat bombs" and butter-loaded drinks add directly to body fat.
why: Dietary fat is absorbed and stored without the insulin step that carbohydrate needs. Natural fat dressing a meal is fine; extra fat for its own sake isn't.

claim: For prediabetes you can cut a carb's insulin effect without cutting carbs: less processed versions, cooked-then-cooled starch, vinegar, eat carbs last, earlier in the day.
why: Same food, different processing and context: steel-cut oats spike glucose less than instant; cooling cooked rice or potatoes creates resistant starch.
do: Pick one or two levers at each meal; combined, they substantially blunt the spike.

claim: Instant oatmeal for breakfast led children to eat more later in the day than the same oats less processed, or an omelet.
why: The fast glucose spike from refined carbs triggers a crash and hunger by mid-morning, which drives extra eating. Processing, not calories, set off the chain.

claim: If fasting stops bringing your blood sugar down, ask your doctor about LADA, a slow-onset autoimmune diabetes often mistaken for type 2.
why: In LADA insulin is low, not high, so fasting (which works by lowering insulin) helps far less, and ketoacidosis becomes a risk.
do: A fasting insulin or C-peptide test and diabetes antibody tests can tell them apart.

claim: Fasting is a stress, like exercise. The right dose strengthens you; too much on top of life stress can push blood sugar the wrong way.
why: Fasting raises cortisol to release stored sugar. With heavy emotional stress it can overwhelm the benefit; backing off can then improve results.
do: In a high-stress period, shorten fasts rather than pushing harder.
note: Fung here says fasting raises cortisol; in CGF ch5 he says short fasts don't. Both fit the evidence: short fasts show little change, longer fasts amplify cortisol (see CGF-05-012 counter).

claim: Rapid weight loss raises the risk of gallstones. Eat some natural fat at meals to keep the gallbladder emptying.
why: Bile left sitting in an unused gallbladder can crystallize into stones. Very low-fat diets and fast weight loss both increase stasis.
do: With known gallstones or past gallbladder attacks, check with your doctor before long fasts. Shorter fasts with normal meals are lower risk.
counter: Fung says there are no good fasting-specific studies; rapid-weight-loss data come from very low-calorie diets and bariatric surgery.

claim: How quickly ketones rise in a first long fast varies widely: some people are in deep ketosis within a day, others take about three.
why: "Metabolic flexibility," the speed of switching from glucose to fat, differs by fitness and metabolic health. Slow switchers feel a low-energy gap.
do: If you're a slow switcher, build up with shorter fasts and lower-carb eating; flexibility improves with practice.

claim: In rats, fasting slowed cyst growth in polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Whether it works in people isn't known yet.
why: Fasting switches off insulin and mTOR growth signaling; the fast-growing kidney cysts appear to respond.
counter: Animal data plus early human pilots. Kidney patients need their nephrologist's guidance (YT-04-004).

claim: On thyroid medication, recheck your thyroid levels when you start fasting or lose weight: the dose you need may drop.
why: Weight loss and calmer autoimmune inflammation can lower the requirement; symptoms are a poor guide, so an unchanged dose can tip you into over-replacement.
do: Racing heart, anxiety, heat intolerance or poor sleep while fasting on thyroid pills: get labs checked.
counter: Reports of fasting improving Hashimoto's are anecdotal; no trials.

claim: With Hashimoto's or hypothyroidism, fast when levels are optimal. While your dose is being adjusted, stick to meals without snacks rather than long fasts.
why: Dose changes take ~5–6 weeks to show in labs. Long fasts during that unstable window make symptoms and levels harder to read and correct.

claim: Fung estimates the "autophagy sweet spot" at roughly 20–30 hours, with longer fasts shifting mostly to fat burning.
why: His reasoning: protein recycling peaks while glucose still comes partly from amino acids, then falls as ketones take over.
counter: An estimate, not a measurement. It conflicts with the app's 24–48 h autophagy stage and "optimal autophagy" framing; human timing is unknown (CGF-07-008).
note: STAGE AUDIT input: even Fung's own estimates vary (book: 24 h+, videos: 16–30 h, here: 20–30 h).

claim: Use a fasting aid only when it decides whether you finish. Ask: "Will this help me fast another 12 hours?"
why: A tablespoon of olive oil can rescue a fast; taken out of habit, aids just add energy that stored fat would otherwise have supplied.

claim: On days 3–5 of a long fast, cravings are mostly mental (food thoughts, ads, smells) rather than physical hunger.
why: Physical hunger has typically faded by then, but food cues everywhere keep triggering desire. A few vegetables or a spoon of fat can quiet it.

claim: Bones get stronger only under load. Walking, stairs and resistance training protect bone far more than calcium pills do.
why: Bone remodels in response to mechanical stress; astronauts lose bone despite eating well. Daily movement matters as much as gym sessions.
do: Combine fasting with regular weight-bearing activity, sun exposure for vitamin D, and nutrient-dense meals.
counter: Fung's Japan comparison (less calcium, fewer fractures) ignores genetics and hip geometry. Calcium and vitamin D still matter if deficient.

claim: The 2024 headline "8-hour eating raises heart-death risk by 91%" came from an unreviewed conference abstract based on two days of diet recall.
why: Participants weren't intentionally fasting, eating windows were self-reported twice over years, and confounders were unclear. That's weak evidence for harm.
counter: AHA's own reviewer (C. Gardner) flagged the same limits: two days of diet recall, no diet-quality or baseline comparison. Check for a later peer-reviewed version before quoting numbers.
note: VERIFIED via AHA newsroom (18 Mar 2024): NHANES 2003–18, ~20,000 adults, two 24-h recalls, preliminary and not peer-reviewed.

claim: Home HbA1c test kits are reasonably accurate, within roughly 6–8% of lab values, and can track progress monthly.
why: HbA1c reflects ~3 months of average blood sugar; monthly home checks show trends sooner, though at extra cost.

claim: Don't drink alcohol during a fast. It blocks the liver's glucose production, so blood sugar can drop, and it hits much harder.
why: The liver prioritizes clearing alcohol and stops gluconeogenesis, so lows can follow, especially on diabetes drugs. An empty stomach raises blood alcohol fast.
do: If you drink, have it with a meal on an eating day, and drink water alongside.

claim: Alcohol undermines results even on eating days: it disrupts sleep, adds empty energy and acts as a diuretic.
why: Poor sleep raises appetite and stress hormones. Many people find weight comes off more easily during an alcohol-free month.

claim: With diabetes or on medication, religious dry fasts need a plan from your doctor, and many traditions allow exemptions or water for health reasons.
why: Water and food restriction together raise risks of dehydration, low blood sugar and low blood pressure; Ramadan guidelines stratify risk and adjust medications.
note: Directly relevant to the lunar fast-day feature (nirjala fasts).

claim: Can't change what you eat? Changing when still helps a lot. Won't fast? Better food still helps. Together they go furthest.
why: Clinic cases improved substantially with fasting on poor diets, and with good diets without fasting, but each alone typically stalled at 70–80% of the goal.

claim: Pateguana ranks the levers: how often you eat first, what time you eat second, what you eat third, then stress and sleep.
why: Her rationale: frequent eating keeps insulin up whatever the food, late eating meets poor insulin sensitivity, and food quality, stress and sleep complete the picture.

claim: Start group support or coaching from day one. You don't need to understand the science first.
why: Accountability, shared tips and regular check-ins make behavior change far more likely, as in any habit program.
note: Overlaps CGF-10-010 and YT-02-013; merge at distillation.

claim: Keep flavored teas and waters (anything listing "natural flavors") for mealtimes; between meals stick to plain water and plain or herbal tea.
why: Undisclosed flavor additives may stimulate appetite and an insulin response; plain drinks keep the fasted state unambiguous.

claim: Feeling cold while fasting is common early on and usually fades as your body gets better at burning fat. Layer up, drink hot, move.
why: New fasters can lag in switching to fat fuel; movement uses circulating fuel and generates heat. With consistency many go from too cold to warm.
do: If you're cold all the time even when not fasting, or it's severe, ask your doctor to check thyroid function.
counter: Feeling cold can also signal under-eating (low energy availability) or hypothyroidism.

claim: If high ketones or low-normal sugar make you feel off during a longer fast, a short walk or a few flights of stairs often helps.
why: Movement uses up circulating ketones and fatty acids; coaches report it settles the "too much fuel, not using it" feeling.

claim: Trying to conceive? Avoid extended fasts after ovulation; focus on full, nourishing meals with a simple eating window instead.
why: You won't know yet if you're pregnant in the second half of the cycle, and pregnancy is a reason not to fast.

claim: The premenstrual week is the hardest time to fast; insulin sensitivity dips and cravings rise. Shorten fasts and avoid sweeteners or extra cream between meals.
why: Insulin sensitivity is lower in the luteal phase; "feeding" cravings with sweet-tasting aids tends to escalate into eating.
do: Fasting usually gets easier again from day 2–3 of your period through ovulation.

claim: The Fasting Method treats 16:8 as maintenance. For fat loss they use 24–48-hour fasts, two or three times a week.
why: Coaches find insulin falls substantially only after about 24 hours; daily 16:8 prevents things worsening but rarely reverses them on its own.
counter: Consistent with RCTs showing modest weight loss with time-restricted eating alone (SCI-12-001). The "24-hour insulin threshold" is clinical impression.

claim: Think of intensive fasting as a time-limited treatment, not a life sentence. Once you've reached your goal, maintenance is much lighter.
why: Clinicians use therapeutic protocols for months, then step down to daily windows plus occasional longer fasts after holidays or stressful periods.

claim: The family cook may prefer two 48-hour fasts a week to three 36s, since that means only two skipped family dinners.
why: Fitting the protocol around household meals improves adherence; total fasted hours are similar.

claim: You can't out-fast an unhealthy diet. What you eat between fasts matters as much as the fasts.
why: Fasting can work for a while despite poor eating, but overeating and processed food between fasts gradually cancel its benefits and make fasts harder.

claim: Still struggling? Look honestly at why and when you eat, and whether it's a want (comfort, habit, company) or a need. No shame.
why: Fasting doesn't change your relationship with food; only noticing and working on the patterns does. Journaling, meditation or therapy can help.
note: Phase-2: optional private note on a fast entry ("what triggered the break?").

claim: Lengthen fasts only once eating between them is steady. If a longer fast leads to overeating, dial back down: not ready yet, not weak.
why: Like moving up to heavier weights, progress sticks when each level is mastered first; jumping ahead invites the fast-then-binge cycle.

claim: A fast that keeps collapsing around hour 20–22 often traces back to the previous day: a carb-heavy meal or simply not eating enough.
why: Refined carbs set up a hunger rebound, and chronic under-eating makes the body push hard for food; both undermine the next fast.
